Then press NUM PAD 5 to read the current cell.</li> </ul> <h5 id="tv-listings-with-both-column-and-row-headers">TV Listings with Both Column and Row Headers</h5> <p>8:00 PM</p> <p>8:30 PM</p> <p>9:00 PM</p> <p>9:30 PM</p> <p>10:00 PM</p> <p>10:30 PM</p> <p>ABC</p> <p>Grey’s Anatomy</p> <p>Scandal</p> <p>How to Get Away with Murder</p> <p>CBS</p> <p>The Big Bang Theory</p> <p>Mom</p> <p>Two and a Half Men</p> <p>The McCarthys</p> <p>Elementary</p> <p>FOX</p> <p>Bones</p> <p>Gracepoint</p> <p>Local Programming</p> <p>NBC</p> <p>The Biggest Loser</p> <p>Bad Judge</p> <p>A to Z</p> <p>Parenthood</p> <p>In the second table the author used table headers for only the first row. The station network names have been omitted from column one. In this case when you use JAWS reading commands to read the current cell you hear the following information:</p> <ul> <li>Column and row position in the table</li> <li>Column header (time)</li> <li>TV show listing from the cell where the cursor currently is located</li> </ul> <h5 id="tv-listings-with-only-column-headers">TV Listings with Only Column Headers</h5> <p>8:00 PM</p> <p>8:30 PM</p> <p>9:00 PM</p> <p>9:30 PM</p> <p>10:00 PM</p> <p>10:30 PM</p> <p>Grey’s Anatomy</p> <p>Scandal</p> <p>How to Get Away with Murder</p> <p>The Big Bang Theory</p> <p>Mom</p> <p>Two and a Half Men</p> <p>The McCarthys</p> <p>Elementary</p> <p>Bones</p> <p>American Idol</p> <p>Fox 5 News at 10</p> <p>The Biggest Loser</p> <p>Bad Judge</p> <p>A to Z</p> <p>Parenthood</p> <p>The third table is just like the first table, except the author did NOT use table headers to mark up the HTML. In this case, you can change JAWS to read them.</p> <h5 id="tv-listings-with-column-and-row-headers-that-are-not-marked-up-properly">TV Listings with Column and Row Headers that are not Marked up Properly</h5> <p>8:00 PM</p> <p>8:30 PM</p> <p>9:00 PM</p> <p>9:30 PM</p> <p>10:00 PM</p> <p>10:30 PM</p> <p>ABC</p> <p>Grey’s Anatomy</p> <p>Scandal</p> <p>How to Get Away with Murder</p> <p>CBS</p> <p>The Big Bang Theory</p> <p>Mom</p> <p>Two and a Half Men</p> <p>The McCarthys</p> <p>Elementary</p> <p>FOX</p> <p>Bones</p> <p>Gracepoint</p> <p>Local Programming</p> <p>NBC</p> <p>The Biggest Loser</p> <p>Bad Judge</p> <p>A to Z</p> <p>Parenthood</p> <p>EXERCISE: Follow the steps below to tell JAWS to read both column and row headers for the table above that does not have proper markup:</p> <ul> <li><p>Press INSERT+V to open the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box while the Tables page is still in the foreground. The Quick Settings dialog box opens with focus in the search edit box.</p></li> <li><p>Type table titles in the edit box. The tree view below filters out all items not related to table titles.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the item Table Titles in the tree view. You should hear JAWS announce “Only Marked Headers.”</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR to change this to Table Titles - Both Row and Column</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. The Quick Settings dialog box closes.</p></li> <li><p>Navigate to the table above and try reading it again. You can press SHIFT+T to move to the prior table. Does it make more sense this time?</p></li> <li><p>Set the Quick Settings back to Table Titles Announce - Only Marked Headers again when you are finished. The fourth table has only the times listed across the top. The network names that were in the first column have been removed. Again, the author did NOT use table headers to mark up the HTML. When you read the current cell you hear only the following information:</p></li> <li><p>Column and row position in the table</p></li> <li><p>TV show listing from the current cell Because the table is not marked up properly, JAWS does not read the column headers.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="tv-listings-with-only-column-headers-that-are-not-marked-up-properly">TV Listings with Only Column Headers that are not Marked Up Properly</h5> <p>8:00 PM</p> <p>8:30 PM</p> <p>9:00 PM</p> <p>9:30 PM</p> <p>10:00 PM</p> <p>10:30 PM</p> <p>Grey’s Anatomy</p> <p>Scandal</p> <p>How to Get Away with Murder</p> <p>The Big Bang Theory</p> <p>Mom</p> <p>Two and a Half Men</p> <p>The McCarthys</p> <p>Elementary</p> <p>Bones</p> <p>Gracepoint</p> <p>Local Programming</p> <p>The Biggest Loser</p> <p>Bad Judge</p> <p>A to Z</p> <p>Parenthood</p> <p>When you encounter this type of table you can change how JAWS reads column and row headers. In this case, you know that the information in row one, at the top of each column, is header information, even though it is not properly marked up. You also know that you do NOT want to have the first column treated as row headers.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Follow the steps below to tell JAWS to read only column headers for the table above that does not have proper markup:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+V to open the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box while the Tables page is still in the foreground. The Quick Settings dialog box opens with focus in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type table titles in the edit box. The tree view below filters out all items not related to table titles.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the item Table Titles in the tree view. You should hear JAWS announce “Only Marked Headers.”</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to change this to Table Titles - Columns</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. The Quick Settings dialog box closes.</li> <li>Navigate to the table above and try reading it again. You can press SHIFT+T to move to the prior table. Does it make more sense this time?</li> <li>Set the JAWS Quick Settings Option back to Table Titles Announce - Only Marked Headers again when you are finished.</li> </ul> <h5 id="document-presentation-mode">Document Presentation Mode</h5> <p>There are two different document presentation modes that you can use when reading tables with JAWS: Simple Layout and Screen Layout. With Simple Layout, each cell of the table is displayed on a separate line in the virtual buffer. Screen Layout mode allows you to read tables by row, just as they are presented on the screen. With Screen Layout each row of the table is displayed on a separate line and each cell is separated by a vertical bar. This lets you get a much better idea about how the table is structured and how different cells in a row relate to each other.</p> <p>Screen Layout mode is also helpful when you want to copy an entire table row and paste it into another document as a single line. The default document presentation mode for JAWS is Simple Layout.</p> <h6 id="to-enable-screen-layout-mode-for-the-current-web-browser-do-the-following">To enable Screen Layout mode for the current web browser, do the following:</h6> <ul> <li>In your browser, press INSERT+V. The Quick Settings dialog box opens with focus in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type document presentation in the search edit box. The tree view below filters out everything that does not relate to document presentation.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW until focus moves to Document Presentation Mode.</li> <li>Press the SPACEBAR to choose Screen Layout.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then SPACEBAR to activate it. NOTE: By default, the quick settings for JAWS are saved to your computer hard disk, and remain set this way until you change them back or to a different setting.</li> </ul> <p>When you practice reading tables with JAWS in the following section, experiment with Screen Layout mode and Simple Layout mode to see which you like best.</p> <h6 id="permanently-enable-screen-layout-mode-for-all-html-and-pdf-tables">Permanently Enable Screen Layout Mode for all HTML and PDF Tables</h6> <p>If you determine that Screen Layout mode is better suited to your needs, you can do the following to permanently enable this feature in HTML and PDF tables.</p> <ul> <li>In your browser, press INSERT+F2.</li> <li>Select Settings Center and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+D to switch to the Default, all files, setting. You can read the title bar of Settings Center to verify this by pressing INSERT+T.</li> <li>Focus is in the Search edit box. Type in “select layout” without the quotes.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Select Layout in the filtered results of the tree view in Settings Center.</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to toggle from Simple Layout to Screen Layout.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. The changes are made and saved. Settings Center closes.</li> </ul> <h5 id="practice-with-more-tables">Practice with More Tables</h5> <p>The next table on this page discusses air and water temperatures for the Tampa Bay area. The Tampa Bay area enjoys an average of 361 days of sunshine a year. The Guinness Book of World records credits Saint Petersburg with the longest run of consecutive sunny days: 768. All the sunshine makes it easy to enjoy the area’s beaches, which include two of the top ten rated beaches in the nation.</p> <h5 id="average-temperatures-for-saint-petersburg">Average Temperatures for Saint Petersburg</h5> <p>Month</p> <p>High Air Temperature</p> <p>Low Air Temperature</p> <p>Gulf Water Temperature</p> <p>January</p> <p>70 degrees</p> <p>50 degrees</p> <p>64 degrees</p> <p>February</p> <p>71 degrees</p> <p>51 degrees</p> <p>65 degrees</p> <p>March</p> <p>77 degrees</p> <p>58 degrees</p> <p>69 degrees</p> <p>April</p> <p>81 degrees</p> <p>61 degrees</p> <p>73 degrees</p> <p>May</p> <p>88 degrees</p> <p>67 degrees</p> <p>79 degrees</p> <p>June</p> <p>89 degrees</p> <p>71 degrees</p> <p>82 degrees</p> <p>July</p> <p>90 degrees</p> <p>75 degrees</p> <p>84 degrees</p> <p>August</p> <p>90 degrees</p> <p>75 degrees</p> <p>86 degrees</p> <p>September</p> <p>89 degrees</p> <p>73 degrees</p> <p>82 degrees</p> <p>October</p> <p>82 degrees</p> <p>65 degrees</p> <p>78 degrees</p> <p>November</p> <p>78 degrees</p> <p>56 degrees</p> <p>71 degrees</p> <p>December</p> <p>72 degrees</p> <p>50 degrees</p> <p>64 degrees</p> <p>The information above is taken from the Chamber of Commerce Web site in Saint Petersburg.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Try re-reading the previous table using Screen Layout mode instead of Simple Layout mode. If you need a reminder about how to switch document presentation modes, see the <a href="ScreenLayout.htm">steps for switching to Screen Layout mode</a>. When you are finished, change JAWS back to Simple Layout mode.</p> <p>Surf’s Up also makes use of cascading style sheets (CSS) for formatting purposes. Using CSS is a best practice technique for Web designers and is the best way to accomplish formatting. One of the formatting techniques used in Surf’s Up is to have cells that are classified as table header elements colored with a lemon yellow background, which is darker than the ivory background of the other table cells.</p> <p>The table below is an example of a table that uses the ID, AXIS, and HEADERS attributes to make JAWS speak different information when navigating different areas of the table. For example, when moving up and down the Employee Name column, you hear the division name as the row header. However, when moving up and down the Phone Extension column, you hear the employee name as the row header. The employee name is actually in column two, but the HTML code is telling JAWS to treat it as the row header in this case, rather than the text in column one. In this case, JAWS reads properly without you having to change any settings for JAWS, since the author of the table took the time to use good practices for coding the HTML of the table. Any given cell can reference any other cell (or cells) anywhere in the table as a header using this technique.</p> <h6 id="employee-extensions-and-departments">Employee Extensions and Departments</h6> <p>Division Name</p> <p>Employee Name</p> <p>Phone Extension</p> <p>Shipping</p> <p>John Smith</p> <p>543</p> <p>Receiving</p> <p>Lee Johnson</p> <p>123</p> <p>Accounting</p> <p>Sharon Jones</p> <p>222</p> <p>This next table is much more complex, but notice how JAWS reads it. When moving up and down column two, where the company name is, the row header information is gathered from column one, the region. When moving up or down any column from three to eight, the row header information is gathered from column two, the company name. You also hear the axis attribute spoken with the words “Region” and “Where.”</p> <h6 id="sales-contacts-by-state">Sales Contacts by State</h6> <p>Company</p> <p>Address</p> <p>City</p> <p>State</p> <p>Phone Number</p> <p>Fax</p> <p>Products</p> <p>West</p> <p>Screen Readers Unlimited</p> <p>52 Third Ave.</p> <p>Los Angeles</p> <p>CA</p> <p>555-555-1234</p> <p>949-555-0101</p> <p>Screen Readers</p> <p>Access Now</p> <p>115 Webb Street</p> <p>Seattle</p> <p>WA</p> <p>206-555-7777</p> <p>206-555-7778</p> <p>Software; Braille Displays; Embossers; Notetakers</p> <p>Webb Access Group</p> <p>100 Main Street</p> <p>Phoenix</p> <p>AZ</p> <p>602-555-3131</p> <p>602-555-3132</p> <p>Software; Web Accessibility Consulting</p> <p>Accessible World</p> <p>5 N. 7th Street</p> <p>San Francisco</p> <p>CA</p> <p>1-800-555-2190</p> <p>Software; Braille Displays; Embossers; Notetakers</p> <p>Midwest</p> <p>Special Computers, Inc.</p> <p>121 4th Street, Suite I</p> <p>Chicago</p> <p>IL</p> <p>800-555-1478</p> <p>708-555-2221</p> <p>Software; Braille Displays; Embossers; Notetakers</p> <p>IndyPendence Day Computing</p> <p>2110 Freedom Dr.</p> <p>Indianapolis</p> <p>IN</p> <p>1-800-555-1332</p> <p>317-555-6261</p> <p>Software; Braille Displays; Embossers; Notetakers</p> <p>Touch the World, Inc.</p> <p>82 S. Broadway</p> <p>Cincinnati</p> <p>OH</p> <p>1-800-555-3691</p> <p>513-555-2221</p> <p>Software; Braille Displays; Embossers; Notetakers</p> <p>In the following table, the first row actually spans the entire width of the table, across all five columns. JAWS uses the COLSPAN and SCOPE attributes to determine how it should read the information in the table. Try reading this table now.</p> <h5 id="sales-report">Sales Report</h5> <p>Produce On Sale</p> <p>First Week</p> <p>Second Week</p> <p>Third Week</p> <p>Fourth Week</p> <p>January</p> <p>Apples</p> <p>Pears</p> <p>Oranges</p> <p>Grapes</p> <p>February</p> <p>Mangos</p> <p>Tangerines</p> <p>Strawberries</p> <p>Kiwis</p> <p>March</p> <p>Cherries</p> <p>Limes</p> <p>Lemons</p> <p>Melons</p> <h3 id="introduction-to-browsing-the-web">Introduction to Browsing the Web</h3> <h4 id="introduction-to-browsing-the-web-1">Introduction to Browsing the Web</h4> <p>Web browsers are programs that allow you to access web pages on the Internet, read HTML (hypertext markup language) documents on your computer, or view your local intranet site. These browsers don’t just display information. They also help you find information using search engines, purchase products online using various online shopping sites, interact with other people using social media services, use web-based editing applications to create documents, and much more.</p> <p>JAWS works best with the latest versions of Microsoft® Edge®, Google Chrome™, and Mozilla® Firefox®. JAWS provides the same powerful features for each supported browser, allowing you to choose the one that best suits your needs.</p> <p>When browsing the web, JAWS gives you quick access to the information you need, and provides detailed information about the structure and organization of web pages. Tables, lists, headings, and alternate text for images are all announced. The information comes right from the HTML used to create the page. HTML is designed with accessibility in mind, and JAWS supports more of the built-in HTML accessibility features than any other screen reader.</p> <p>JAWS uses the Virtual Cursor on web pages, letting you read as you would in a word processing document. The Virtual Cursor is also available in other applications, such as HTML based help systems, HTML based e-mails in Outlook, and in PDF (Portable Document Format) files. Many of the features discussed within these topics are also available wherever the Virtual Cursor is used.</p> <p>When you open the browser, your home page opens. If you don’t have a home page specified, you can select a web page from your list of favorites, or press ALT+D to move to the Address Bar and type in the address of a page. Once a page is selected, it is loaded and JAWS announces the page title along with the number of links, headings, and regions. Then, JAWS begins reading the text on the screen from top to bottom. To move through the page, use UP and DOWN ARROW, PAGE UP, and PAGE DOWN as you would in a word processing document. The JAWS commands to Read By Word, Line, Sentence, and Paragraph work normally.</p> <p>Tip: If you are using Fusion, JAWS will not automatically begin reading the page after announcing the title followed by the number of elements. This prevents focus from being bumped back up to the top of the page if you are a low vision user attempting to navigate with the mouse. To change this setting, open JAWS Settings Center and select “Document and Web Pages Automatically Read.”</p> <p>As you navigate a page, JAWS says, “link,” when it encounters a link to another document or portion of the page. To follow a link, press ENTER while positioned on the link.</p> <p>To go back to the previous page, press ALT+LEFT ARROW or BACKSPACE. To move forward one page after you have moved back, press ALT+RIGHT ARROW.</p> <h3 id="jaws-reading-commands">JAWS Reading Commands</h3> <h4 id="jaws-reading-commands-1">JAWS Reading Commands</h4> <p>The following is a list of the JAWS commands for reading text. To close this page, press CTRL+F4.</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Prior Character</p> <p>LEFT ARROW</p> <p>Next Character</p> <p>RIGHT ARROW</p> <p>Current Character</p> <p>NUM PAD 5</p> <p>Say Character Phonetically</p> <p>NUM PAD 5 twice quickly</p> <p>Prior Word</p> <p>INSERT+LEFT ARROW</p> <p>Next Word</p> <p>INSERT+RIGHT ARROW</p> <p>Current Word</p> <p>INSERT+NUM PAD 5</p> <p>Spell Word</p> <p>INSERT+NUM PAD 5 twice quickly</p> <p>Prior Line</p> <p>UP ARROW</p> <p>Next Line</p> <p>DOWN ARROW</p> <p>Current Line</p> <p>INSERT+UP ARROW</p> <p>Spell Current Line</p> <p>INSERT+UP ARROW twice quickly</p> <p>Prior Sentence</p> <p>ALT+NUM PAD MINUS</p> <p>Next Sentence</p> <p>ALT+NUM PAD PLUS</p> <p>Current Sentence</p> <p>ALT+NUM PAD 5</p> <p>Prior Paragraph</p> <p>CTRL+UP ARROW</p> <p>Next Paragraph</p> <p>CTRL+DOWN ARROW</p> <p>Current Paragraph</p> <p>CTRL+NUM PAD 5</p> <p>Say to Cursor</p> <p>INSERT+HOME</p> <p>Say from Cursor</p> <p>INSERT+PAGE UP</p> <p>Spell to Cursor</p> <p>INSERT+HOME twice quickly</p> <p>Spell from Cursor</p> <p>INSERT+PAGE UP twice quickly</p> <p>Say All</p> <p>INSERT+DOWN ARROW</p> <p>Fast Forward during a Say All</p> <p>RIGHT ARROW</p> <p>Rewind during a Say All</p> <p>LEFT ARROW</p> <p>Toggle Speech On or Off</p> <p>INSERT+SPACEBAR, S</p> <p>Note: When using this keystroke, press and release INSERT+SPACEBAR, and then press S.</p> <p>Say Color</p> <p>INSERT+5</p> <p>Say ASCII Value</p> <p>NUM PAD 5 three times quickly</p> <p>Say Font</p> <p>INSERT+F</p> <p>Display Font Information in Virtual Viewer</p> <p>INSERT+F twice quickly</p> <p>Start Skim Reading</p> <p>CTRL+INSERT+DOWN ARROW</p> <h3 id="jaws-web-verbosity">JAWS Web Verbosity</h3> <h4 id="jaws-web-verbosity-1">JAWS Web Verbosity</h4> <p>When reading content using the Virtual Cursor, JAWS alerts you to the beginning and end of various elements such as lists, tables, and regions. With JAWS support for ARIA continuing to improve and web developers becoming more aware of accessible design, the amount of extra information provided by the Virtual Cursor can become overwhelming when you just want to focus on the page content. To make it easier to determine what is spoken, JAWS now offers three levels of verbosity for the Virtual Cursor, giving you control over how much detail you want to hear when reading various web content. The three levels are:</p> <ul> <li><p>High - JAWS speaks the most information about elements on the page or inside a document. Everything except the start and end of application and document regions is announced at this level.</p></li> <li><p>Medium - This level is configured to provide the best user experience on most pages and documents and is the default verbosity level. By default, JAWS will not indicate the start and end for flash objects or frames, and only the start and end of navigation and main regions is announced. Note that the name and type for all regions is still announced when using the R and SHIFT+R Navigation Quick Keys to move by region or the O and SHIFT+O Navigation Quick Keys to move by article.</p></li> <li><p>Low - JAWS speaks as little structural information as possible about the elements on a page or inside a document. By default, only the start and end of tables and grids is announced at this level. To choose a verbosity level, do the following:</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+F2, and select Settings Center. Note that since you started Settings Center while your default web browser had focus, the title bar of Settings Center reads, “JAWS Settings Center - <Browser Name>.” This means this setting will only apply when using this particular browser. Should you wish to apply this setting to all web browsers, one would first press the keystroke CTRL+SHIFT+D to change to the default settings before continuing the exercise.</p></li> <li><p>In the Search edit box, type “web verbosity” without the quotes.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to “Web Verbosity Level” in the filtered search results in the tree view.</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR to choose the level you want.</p></li> <li><p>Press ENTER to save your change and close Settings Center. You can also choose a Virtual Cursor verbosity level to be active for a specific website. From the website where you want to use a different verbosity level, press INSERT+V to open Quick Settings, navigate to the Personalized Web Settings group, and press SPACEBAR on Virtual Cursor Verbosity Level to choose the verbosity level you want for the current site.</p></li> </ul> <p>Each verbosity level is preset to provide the most optimal experience. However, just like with speech verbosity, each level can be further customized to give only the information you want to hear. For example, you may want to continue using the default Medium verbosity level, but you may want JAWS to announce a few more elements that are not spoken by default at this level.</p> <h5 id="change-web-verbosity-to-look-for-more-at-medium-verbosity-level---practice">Change Web Verbosity to Look for More at Medium Verbosity Level - Practice</h5> <p>EXERCISE: Configure JAWS to announce the Content Information region at the bottom of each Surf’s Up page as you navigate with the arrow keys. Content Information regions are not indicated by default at the Medium verbosity level.</p> <ul> <li><p>Press INSERT+F2, and select Settings Center.</p></li> <li><p>In the Search edit box, type “web verbosity” without the quotes.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to “Configure Web Verbosity Levels” in the filtered search results in the tree view and press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Press RIGHT ARROW to expand the “Configure Web Verbosity Levels” group.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Medium and press SPACEBAR. A dialog box opens containing a tree view listing the structural elements that can be announced by the Virtual Cursor. Tip: Pressing TAB one time moves you to a read-only text area containing a description of the currently selected element in the tree view.</p></li> <li><p>You can use the arrow keys to explore all of the items in this tree view or press R to jump directly to the Regions node.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW until you reach Content Information and press SPACEBAR to check this region type.</p></li> <li><p>Press ENTER to activate the OK button. Focus returns to Settings Center.</p></li> <li><p>Press ALT+A to activate the Apply button in Settings Center. Activating the Apply button allows you to make instant changes to settings without having to close the Settings Center dialog box. That way we can change the setting back in just a minute without having to re-open Settings Center. Now, press ALT+TAB to return to the JAWS Web Verbosity page. Settings Center is still running in the background and is still open. Press DOWN ARROW until you hear JAWS say “Main Region End.” Continue pressing DOWN ARROW and you should hear JAWS say “Content Information,” followed by the Back and Next links, and finally “Content Information End.”</p></li> </ul> <p>Repeat this exercise if you want to try selecting or clearing other elements that you may or may not want to have announced as you navigate pages.</p> <h5 id="change-web-verbosity-back-to-default-setting">Change Web Verbosity Back to Default Setting</h5> <ul> <li>Press ALT+TAB to switch back to Settings Center.</li> <li>This time, let’s use the Last Changed Settings item in Settings Center to revert the change. Press END to move to the bottom of the tree view in Settings Center. JAWS should announce it as “Last Changed Settings, closed.”</li> <li>Press RIGHT ARROW to open the tree node, and then press DOWN ARROW to move to “Medium… (Web / HTML / PDFs ,Reading,Configure Web Verbosity Levels).”</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to reopen the dialog box containing a tree view listing the structural elements that can be announced by the Virtual Cursor.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW until you reach Content Information and press SPACEBAR to uncheck this region type.</li> <li>Press ENTER to activate the OK button. Focus returns to Settings Center.</li> <li>Finally, press ENTER once more to close Settings Center.</li> </ul> <h3 id="languages-with-jaws-on-the-internet">Languages with JAWS on the Internet</h3> <h4 id="languages-with-jaws-on-the-internet-1">Languages with JAWS on the Internet</h4> <p>JAWS provides language switching with any supported speech synthesizer. When a Web page author indicates the language of an entire page, or just part of a page, if the synthesizer in use supports that language, JAWS uses the language specific version of the synthesizer to speak the text. The synthesizer must support the language of the information.</p> <p>If the synthesizer does not support the language specified for a page or part of a page, JAWS still indicates the language of the information.</p> <p>To demonstrate automatic language detection, we start in English and write:</p> <p>“My computer speaks English.”</p> <p>Then we write the same sentence in French,</p> <p>mon ordinateur parle français</p> <p>and then in Spanish,</p> <p>mi computadora habla español</p> <p>and in Portuguese,</p> <p>meu computador fala o português</p> <p>and the same in German,</p> <p>mein computer spricht deutsch</p> <p>and in Russian,</p> <p>Мой компьютер говорит по-русски</p> <p>and in Finnish,</p> <p>Tietokoneeni puhuu suomea</p> <p>and in Italian,</p> <p>il mio computer parla italiano</p> <p>and in Greek,</p> <p>Ο υπολογιστής μου μηλάει ελληνικά,</p> <p>and in Polish,</p> <p>Mój komputer mówi po polsku</p> <p>and in Chinese,</p> <p>我的電腦說中文</p> <p>JAWS switches between the languages very smoothly, when it can. If JAWS only said, “Russian,” “Greek,” or “Polish,” instead of reading the text in those languages, this indicates that your speech synthesizer (Eloquence, for example) does not support those languages. If you are using Vocalizer Expressive, it indicates that you do not have those particular voices installed.</p> <p>JAWS includes a utility that makes it easy to seamlessly sample and install or remove Vocalizer Expressive 2 premium voices. To install Vocalizer Expressive voices, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+J to open the JAWS application window.</li> <li>Press ALT+O to open the Options menu, expand the Voices submenu, and then select Add/Remove Voices to open the Add/Remove Vocalizer Expressive Voices utility.</li> <li>In the Select a Language combo box, select the language that you want to download voices for.</li> <li>In the Premium Voices list box, press the SPACEBAR on the voices you want to install. You can select as many voices as you like. To hear a sample of the current voice before deciding if you want to select it, press ALT+P.</li> <li>Select the Install Selected Voices button to begin the installation.</li> </ul> <h3 id="mathml">MathML</h3> <h4 id="mathml-1">MathML</h4> <p>MathML (Mathematical Markup Language) is a W3C (World Wide Web Consortium) recommendation of a markup language for displaying both mathematical structure as well as content, or meaning. JAWS and Fusion provide spoken, natural language descriptions of MathML equations, using the same terms a teacher would use to explain them in a classroom. This enables students to read and study math problems contained in web pages using both speech and braille.</p> <p>JAWS supports reading math content in Edge, Chrome, and Firefox that is created using MathML without the need to install any additional third-party software applications or plugins. Everything happens on the developer side. Visit the <a href="https://www.w3.org/Math">W3 website</a> to learn more about MathML and the tools used to add it to web pages.</p> <p>If a refreshable braille display is connected, JAWS also shows math expressions on the display using the Nemeth Braille code, a widely used system for reading math in braille. Since Nemeth Braille is exclusive to English, make sure JAWS is configured for one of the English contracted braille output modes by doing the following:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+6 on the number row to open Settings Center.</li> <li>To apply changes to all applications, press CTRL+SHIFT+D to load the JAWS default settings. To apply changes to a specific application, select it from the Applications combo box.</li> <li>In the Search edit box, type “Translation” without the quotes.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Translation in the filtered search results in the tree view and press ENTER to move focus to the Translation group. Press RIGHT ARROW to expand the group.</li> <li>In the Language combo box, make sure English – United States is selected.</li> <li>In the Output combo box, make sure one of the Grade 1 or Grade 2 options is selected.</li> <li>Select OK to save your changes and close Settings Center. Tip: If you are using a Freedom Scientific Focus Blue braille display, you can press DOTS 1-2-4-5-7-8 CHORD to quickly switch to contracted braille.</li> </ul> <h5 id="actively-explore-math-content-with-jaws">Actively Explore Math Content with JAWS</h5> <p>When you encounter MathML on a web page, JAWS describes the equation, followed by the message “math content.” If you are using a braille display and JAWS is configured for Contracted Braille, the message “Math” is displayed followed by the expression. If the expression is too long to fit on the display, you can use the panning buttons on your display to view the rest of it. Otherwise, if JAWS is set for Computer Braille, the message “Math” is displayed followed by a message stating that Contracted Braille must be enabled to view math content.</p> <p>Pressing ENTER while focused on the math content opens the JAWS Math Viewer where you can study the equation in greater detail by doing the following:</p> <ul> <li>To move between parts of the expression, use the LEFT and RIGHT ARROW keys.</li> <li>To focus in on a partial expression, press DOWN ARROW.</li> <li>To return to the prior level, press UP ARROW.</li> <li>To read all the partial expressions at the current level, press INSERT+UP ARROW.</li> <li>To read the current partial expression or term, press NUM PAD 5 or INSERT+NUM PAD 5.</li> <li>From within the Math Viewer, press ESC or ALT+F4 to exit. Our goal with JAWS math support is to allow you to navigate the math content by logically grouped elements. For example, a fraction consists of a numerator and a denominator. Both the numerator and denominator may consist of sub-expressions. We give you the ability to navigate between the numerator and the denominator, and then by sub-expression if desired.</li> </ul> <h5 id="description-of-math-equations-by-jaws">Description of Math Equations by JAWS</h5> <p>We want the screen reader’s description of a given equation to be as close to what a teacher would say in a classroom as possible. For example, x2/-y could accurately be described as, “x to the power of 2 divided by minus y,” but a teacher might say “x squared over negative y.”</p> <p>Following is an example math expression. Press ENTER on the math content to open it in the Math Viewer and then use the ARROW keys to explore it.</p> <p>x + 1 − 1 3</p> <h5 id="practice-with-more-examples">Practice with More Examples</h5> <p>EXERCISE: Follow the steps below to explore the quadratic formula example on the MathML examples page.</p> <p><a href="MathML-Samples.html">MathML examples page Opens a new window</a></p> <ul> <li>First, navigate to the line where the quadratic formula is. When you hear JAWS announce “math content,” press ENTER to open the JAWS Math Viewer.</li> <li>Press the JAWS Say Line keystroke, INSERT+UP ARROW. JAWS reads the entire formula.</li> <li>Press LEFT and RIGHT ARROW to move to the different subcomponents at the current level. Beginning at the left, you should hear the following, each separately: <ul> <li>x</li> <li>=</li> <li>negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, over 2 a</li> </ul></li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the numerator subcomponent. JAWS reads the following: <ul> <li>negative b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, numerator</li> </ul></li> <li>Press RIGHT ARROW to move to the denominator subcomponent. JAWS reads the following: <ul> <li>2a, denominator</li> </ul></li> <li>Press LEFT ARROW to move back to the numerator part of the expression, and then press DOWN ARROW to move to the subcomponents within the numerator. JAWS reads the following: <ul> <li>negative b</li> </ul></li> <li>Press RIGHT ARROW to move through the different subcomponents of the numerator. JAWS reads the following: <ul> <li>plus or minus</li> <li>b squared minus 4 a c, under square root</li> </ul></li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to explore the subcomponents at the next level. JAWS reads the following: <ul> <li>b squared</li> </ul></li> <li>Press RIGHT ARROW to move through the different parts of the expression. JAWS reads the following: <ul> <li>minus</li> <li>4 a c</li> </ul></li> <li>Press LEFT ARROW to move back to the first part of the expression, b squared, and then press DOWN ARROW to move to the subcomponents at the next level.</li> <li>Press LEFT and RIGHT ARROW to read them. JAWS reads them separately as follows: <ul> <li>b</li> <li>2 exponent</li> </ul></li> <li>Press UP ARROW to move out of the subcomponents back to the prior level. JAWS says b squared.</li> <li>Press RIGHT ARROW to move to the right until JAWS says 4 a c, and then press DOWN ARROW to move to the subcomponent level for this part of the expression. JAWS says 4.</li> <li>Press RIGHT ARROW to explore and notice JAWS speaks the following items: a c If you are sighted, you should see the contents of the Math Viewer displayed visually on the screen. As the equation is navigated, the current expression or partial expression is highlighted so a sighted teacher can easily tell what part of the expression is being spoken.</li> </ul> <p>If you are using a braille display, notice that the entire equation remains on the display as you use the ARROW keys to explore it. However, the cursor (dots 7 and 8) moves to the start of the partial expression that gains focus. Pressing a Cursor Router over a term in the equation immediately moves the cursor to the specific location and causes JAWS to speak and visually highlight the partial expression as if you moved to it with the ARROW keys.</p> <p>When you finish exploring with the ARROW keys and the keystrokes for say character, say word, and say line, press UP ARROW to move back to the main level. Press ESC to close the Math Viewer when you are finished.</p> <p>Feel free to continue to explore some of the other math equations and expressions on the sample page with JAWS. When you are finished, don’t forget to close any open instances of the Math Viewer with either ESC or ALT+F4, and close the sample page with CTRL+F4 as well.</p> <h3 id="navigating-web-pages">Navigating Web Pages</h3> <h4 id="navigating-web-pages-1">Navigating Web Pages</h4> <p>JAWS makes reading web pages easy. When you visit a page JAWS immediately begins reading the page from the top down. In this section, you will learn about <a href="QuickKeys.htm">Navigation Quick Keys</a>, reading text, and navigating headings, lists, links, and images.</p> <h5 id="reading-text">Reading Text</h5> <p>JAWS uses the Virtual Cursor to move through HTML pages, enabling JAWS users to read and select text and move to different elements on the page. The Virtual Cursor is invisible to sighted users, however, JAWS highlights text as it is read so a sighted user such as a teacher, parent, tester, or developer can easily follow the text visually.</p> <p>The commands used to read web pages are the same as the commands used to read text in any other type of document. You can also select and copy text on web pages. The sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> demonstrates the layout and content of a typical web page on the Internet.</p> <p>JAWS Tip: To see a complete list of commands that you can use to read text in documents, refer to the <a href="ReadingCommands.htm">JAWS Reading Commands</a> table. If you are not yet familiar with JAWS table reading commands just press DOWN ARROW to move through and read the commands in the table.</p> <p>JAWS Tip: To begin reading anywhere on a web page beneath the mouse cursor with JAWS, move the mouse pointer over the text you want to read. Then press the keystroke INSERT+NUM PAD PLUS. This is the keystroke to route the virtual cursor to the mouse cursor. Then use normal reading keys.</p> <p>To practice reading text on the Internet with JAWS, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+F7 to display a list of links on this page.</li> <li>Make sure the link <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> is selected and press ENTER. This opens the sample page in a new browser window. You can hold down CTRL and press TAB to switch back to this window and refer to these instructions. JAWS remembers where you are on the page, so you won’t lose your place. If the page opens in a completely new window just use ALT+TAB to switch between windows.</li> <li>When the page loads, JAWS begins reading it. Press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page. Then press P three times to move to the second paragraph on the page. The first press of the letter P on this page moves to the graphic logo and heading level one at the top of the page for Jim’s Cafe.</li> <li>Use the <a href="ReadingCommands.htm">standard JAWS reading commands</a> to read the text on the page. Any command that you can use to read text or Word documents can be used when reading web pages.</li> <li>Press SHIFT+P until you return to the first paragraph on the page. JAWS Tip: The letter P is a Navigation Quick Key that lets you move by paragraph through the page. There are other Navigation Quick Keys that let you move through all the headings, links, images, and other elements on the page. If you hold SHIFT when you press one of these keys, JAWS moves to the previous element. For example, pressing SHIFT+P moves you to the previous paragraph. To read more about them choose the link <a href="QuickKeys.htm">Navigation Quick Keys</a>.</li> </ul> <h6 id="hyperlinks">Hyperlinks</h6> <p>A hyperlink (or “link” for short) is text that performs some action when you click it or select it and press ENTER. You can move through all the links on the page by pressing the TAB key. To see how JAWS helps you navigate links, do the following:</p> <ul> <li><p>Open the sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</p></li> <li><p>Press U to move to the first unvisited link on the page. An unvisited link is one that leads to a page or location that you have not visited.</p></li> <li><p>Press V to move to the next visited link on the page. A visited link is one that you have previously activated or one that leads to a page you have visited recently.</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+F7 to display a list of all links on the page. Use the arrow keys to select “Innisport Hotel” and then press ENTER. Read the message that appears and then press ENTER. NOTE: If the dialog box does not read automatically just press the JAWS keystroke to read the current window, INSERT+B.</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+F7 again. Select “Reputation for Quality Service” and press ALT+M to move to this link. JAWS says, “This page link,” to indicate that this hyperlink will take you to another location on the current page. JAWS Tip: The link “Reputation for Quality Service” is the start of a list of four links. Many web pages use clusters of links like this to consolidate page navigation in a single spot. If you wanted to continue reading down the page without using any of these links, you could skip over them by pressing N. The Navigation Quick Key N moves you to the next block of text that is not a link.</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+F7 again. Select “Send us an e-mail message” and press ALT+M to move to this link. JAWS says, “Send mail link,” to indicate that this link allows you to send a message to an e-mail address using your default mail program.</p></li> </ul> <h6 id="skip-to-main-content-links">Skip to Main Content Links</h6> <p>Some web pages have special links with names like “Skip to Main Content” or “Skip Navigation.” These same page links allow you to quickly jump past site navigation tools, such as menus, navigation bars, and so on and go directly to the important information on the page. These types of links usually appear at the beginning of the page and are often invisible to sighted users.</p> <h5 id="lists">Lists</h5> <p>Web pages often contain bulleted (unordered) and numbered (ordered) lists that provide information. The procedures on this page are examples of lists. To see how JAWS navigates lists, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Open the sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</li> <li>Press L to move to the first list on the page. This is a bulleted list that contains three items.</li> <li>Press I to read the first item on the list. You can continue using either I or the DOWN ARROW key to read through the rest of the list. To move back through the list, use SHIFT+I or the UP ARROW key.</li> <li>Press L to move to the next list. This is a numbered list with four steps that explain how to locate the restaurant. Review the steps in this list with I or the arrow keys.</li> <li>Press I until you move to step three.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the nested list within step three. This nested list is an unordered list of three bulleted items. A nested list is a list of items that is contained within a larger list. Another example of a nested list would be an outline. JAWS announces the level of nested lists. Lists may be arranged differently depending on their purpose. Web page authors may interrupt a list with a paragraph, quote, image, or similar element. If this is the case, the next list on the page usually begins where the previous list ended. For example, if a procedure is interrupted during step three by an image, the next list on the page might begin with step four.</li> </ul> <p>JAWS Tip: You can display all lists on the page by pressing INSERT+CTRL+L. You can then select a list and press ENTER to move to it. Note that the list items within each list are displayed in one single horizontal line per list within this dialog box, so you hear a lot of information when using this particular keystroke.</p> <h5 id="headings">Headings</h5> <p>Web page authors use headings to divide a document into sections. Level 1 is the highest level of heading. Level 2 headings are subsections of level 1 headings. Level 3 headings are subsections of level 2 headings and so on.</p> <h6 id="navigation-quick-keys-for-headings">Navigation Quick Keys for Headings</h6> <p>To see how JAWS allows you to navigate headings, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Open the sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</li> <li>Press H to move to and read the first heading on the page. JAWS says, “Jim’s Cafe at Innisport.” This is the only level one heading on the page. Level one headings often indicate the topic or subject of the page.</li> <li>Press H again until you move to the level three heading, “Poultry.” Press P to read the text below this heading.</li> <li>Press H a few more times. You eventually reach the bottom of the page. JAWS says, “Wrapping to top,” when there are no more headings. JAWS then moves you back to the first heading at the top of the document. JAWS Tip: Don’t forget that you can add SHIFT to navigation quick keys to move backward through the page. For example, press SHIFT+H to move to the previous heading.</li> </ul> <p>When you reach the top of the page by using the SHIFT key in combination with navigation quick keys to move backwards through the page, JAWS announces, “Wrapping to bottom,” and starts over again from the bottom of the document.</p> <p>You can press ALT+INSERT+HOME to move to the first heading on the page, and press ALT+INSERT+END to move to the last heading on the page.</p> <h6 id="using-the-numbers-row-to-jump-to-a-specific-heading-level">Using the Numbers Row to Jump to a Specific Heading Level</h6> <p>You can move to headings of a certain level by pressing a number between 1 and 6 as long as one or more headings of the specified level exist on the web page. To see how this works, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Open the sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</li> <li>Press 1 to move to and read the first heading on the page. JAWS says, “Jim’s Cafe at Innisport.” Press 1 again and notice that JAWS says “No more headings at level 1” since this is the only level one heading on the page.</li> <li>Since we’ve been to this page before, we know that all of the menu items are under level three headings, so we want to quickly jump to these without looking at anything else on the page. Press 3 to move to the first level three heading which is “Poultry.”</li> <li>Did you notice that JAWS first announced the level two heading “Dishes and Appetizers” followed by the level three heading “Poultry?” There is a prior section with a level two heading called “Reputation for Quality Service” which does not contain any level three headings. Since JAWS completely skips over a section of the web page in order to reach the first level three heading, JAWS announces the higher precedence heading, in this case “Dishes and Appetizers,” before announcing the “Poultry” heading so you know you have moved into a new section.</li> <li>Continue pressing the number 3 a few times. Did you hear JAWS announce “no next heading at level three in this section” after reaching the level three heading for Seafood?</li> <li>Now try pressing the number 3 with the SHIFT key to move backwards by level three headings. Did you hear JAWS announce “no prior heading at level three in this section” after reaching the level three heading for Poultry? This gives you a good idea of how the different headings relate to each other. JAWS Tip: You can also choose to have JAWS play a sound to indicate when you move into a new section or you can restrict heading navigation using the numbers row to the current section. For example, if you attempt to move to a level three heading, but the very next heading is a level two, JAWS stops at the level two heading and will not pass it even though there may be level three headings in the next section.</li> </ul> <p>To configure how JAWS navigates headings when using the numbers 1 through 6, open Settings Center, type “heading” into the Search edit box, select the “Heading Navigation Using 1-6” option, and then press SPACEBAR to choose the setting you want. Alternatively, open Quick Settings (INSERT+V) from your browser and configure the “Heading Navigation” setting.</p> <h6 id="the-jaws-list-of-headings">The JAWS List of Headings</h6> <p>JAWS also has a list of headings that allows you to navigate by headings on a web page. You can sort this list by tab order or alphabetically. You can also view only headings of a specified level. To explore the options in this dialog box, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Open the sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</li> <li>Press INSERT+F6 to display a list of headings on this page. Press DOWN ARROW to move through the list and read the headings. If you select a heading and press ENTER, the list closes and you move directly to that heading in the document.</li> <li>Press the TAB key to explore the Heading List dialog box in more detail. Each option is described below: <ul> <li>Move To Heading button - Use this button to move to the location of the currently selected heading.</li> <li>Cancel button - Closes the list of headings without changing your location on the page.</li> <li>Sort Headings radio buttons - Select one of these radio buttons to specify whether you want to sort the headings in this list alphabetically or by tab order.</li> <li>Display radio buttons - Select one of these radio buttons to include only headings of the specified level in the list.</li> </ul></li> <li>Make sure you are back in the actual list of headings. Press ALT+1 on the numbers row and read the current line by pressing INSERT+UP ARROW. You should hear that there is only one item now in the list, a level one heading.</li> <li>Press ALT+2 on the numbers row and read the current line by pressing INSERT+UP ARROW. You should hear that there are now four items displayed in the list, all level two headings. In the list of headings, you can filter out all headings except the specific level you are looking for by pressing ALT and any number from 1 to 6. To view all headings again, press ALT+L.</li> <li>Press ESC for now to close the list of headings. TIP: Use the list of headings in JAWS whenever you first go to a web page to get an overview of how the page is structured.</li> </ul> <h5 id="images">Images</h5> <p>Most web pages use images to enhance their appearance, provide information, or assist with navigation. To see how JAWS handles images, do the following:</p> <ul> <li><p>Open the sample page <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a> and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</p></li> <li><p>Press G until you move to the level one heading, “Jim’s Cafe at Innisport.” You may not have noticed it earlier, but the level one heading in this document is actually an image.</p></li> <li><p>JAWS cannot read graphic text. The text you are hearing for this image is called alternate text. Web page authors use alternate text to describe images.</p></li> <li><p>Press G to move to the next image, which is a graphical link. The alternate text tells you that this is a map. On an actual page, a person might be able to click this image to open another page where the image is shown in larger size.</p></li> <li><p>Press ENTER to activate the graphical link. Read the message that appears and then press ALT+F4. If the dialog box does not read automatically just press the JAWS keystroke to read the current window, INSERT+B.</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+CTRL+G to display a list of all images on the page. This keystroke only works if you have JAWS running. JAWS Tip: When you press INSERT+CTRL+G notice that the item highlighted in the list is the one that is closest to where you are currently reading on the page.</p></li> <li><p>Select the next image, which is an image of the Vispero logo. This one is more than just an image; it is also a graphic link. Additionally, this link has an alt attribute describing the image. The link takes you to the Vispero home page. If you want to activate the link, press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Press G to move to the last image on the page. This image has no alternate text. However, this image is a link to another page. For images like this one, JAWS announces the image’s file name and tells you that the image is a link.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="tab-pages-in-web-browsers">Tab Pages in Web Browsers</h5> <p>You can have several different tab pages open at once in web browsers. You can switch between the multiple tabbed pages by pressing CTRL+TAB. Use the link here for a list of <a href="TabbedBrowsingKeystrokes.htm">keystrokes for tabbed browsing</a>. If you are using a web browser, such as Chrome, Edge Chromium, or Firefox and you want a more complete list of the keystrokes, how would you find out what keystrokes are available to you? You can press INSERT+F1 twice quickly in any application to find the JAWS help for that application. Also, within different applications try pressing INSERT+H to open JAWS Hotkey Help for that application.</p> <p>JAWS Tip: You can use PlaceMarkers with JAWS to mark spots on web pages so that you can find them again quickly. PlaceMarkers are discussed in more detail later, but they are very easy to use. Here’s how to get started with PlaceMarkers:</p> <ul> <li><p>Before moving on, let’s put a PlaceMarker right here. You can move right back to any spot on any web page using JAWS PlaceMarkers. Press CTRL+SHIFT+K. The PlaceMarker dialog box appears. Focus is on the Add button.</p></li> <li><p>Press ENTER to activate the Add button. JAWS gathers the text from where you are on the page and puts it into an edit box. You can change this by typing over it or editing it, but for now, just leave it alone and press ENTER to close the PlaceMarker dialog box.</p></li> <li><p>Press CTRL+HOME to go to the top of the page.</p></li> <li><p>Now press the navigation quick key K to move back to where you just put the PlaceMarker on this page. See how that works? Feel free to put PlaceMarkers anywhere on the Surf’s Up pages as you begin using them. It makes it very easy to get back to the exact spot you want to go to. EXERCISE: Try the following exercise for tabbed browsing now.</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the next link on this page, followed by CTRL+ENTER. The Jim’s Cafe page loads in a new tab page in the background. Navigating Web pages is still running on a tab page in the foreground. <a href="JimsCafe.htm">Jim’s Cafe at Innisport</a></p></li> <li><p>Press CTRL+TAB a few times to move between the two pages.</p></li> <li><p>Next, press CTRL+TAB to move back to the Jim’s Cafe page and spend a minute reading through it. When you are finished, press CTRL+TAB to move back to the Navigating page.</p></li> <li><p>Next, if you are using Firefox or Internet Explorer, press ALT+F4 but don’t go beyond that. If you only had one tab page open ALT+F4 would close that page and the whole browser window. Instead, since there are multiple tab pages open, you should get a message from the browser asking “Do you want to close all tabs?” Since you DO have multiple tab pages open, the browser gives you this prompt.</p></li> <li><p>Press ESC to get out of this dialog box. NOTE: Currently, when you press ALT+F4 in Chrome or Edge Chromium and multiple tabs are opened, the browser closes without displaying a prompt and all pages will be closed.</p></li> <li><p>Press CTRL+TAB a couple of times to make sure you are on the Jim’s Cafe page.</p></li> <li><p>Now press CTRL+F4 to close just that page. Focus returns to the Navigating Web page. NOTE: It is still possible to have multiple instances of each web browser running and each instance can have multiple tabs. If you have two or more different browser sessions running you can press ALT+TAB to move from one session to another. For example, many of the sample pages for Surf’s Up run in separate windows, not as tabbed pages.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="navigation-quick-key-manager">Navigation Quick Key Manager</h5> <p>Navigation Quick Key manager is used to view, edit, or delete Navigation Quick Key assignments. To open Navigation Quick Key manager do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+J to switch to the JAWS window.</li> <li>From within the JAWS window press ALT+U to open the Utilities menu.</li> <li>Press N to open the Navigation Quick Key manager submenu. Focus moves to the first item of three, HTML/PDF.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move through the other two items. You find one for Microsoft Word and one for Microsoft Outlook. NOTE: You can also find Navigation Quick Key Manager in the list of JAWS managers by pressing INSERT+F2.</li> </ul> <h5 id="aria-and-regions">ARIA and Regions</h5> <p>ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) regions can be used to add additional navigation structure to web pages. Web page authors can add regions to web pages to make it easier to find the main parts of a page. For example, you might find a main region which is where the main content of a page begins. You may also find banner, navigation, and search regions on some web pages. When a web page loads, JAWS announces if there are regions on the page. Use the keystroke R to move forward from one region to another. Press SHIFT+R to move backward from one region to another. You may also use the keystroke INSERT+CTRL+R to open a JAWS list of regions for a web page.</p> <p>The Surf’s Up home page has three regions. There is a “main” region which begins near the top of the page. The main region is typically where the primary content of most web pages begins, and should be after, or below, the links that one typically finds near the top of the page for navigation to other parts of the web site. The Surf’s Up home page and the remaining pages of Surf’s Up also have a “content information” region. The content information region on most web sites, including Surf’s Up, is typically the footer of the page and may contain more links and copyright information. We’ve kept the footer of Surf’s Up pretty clean and empty of extra content for now. Finally, on the home page of Surf’s Up only, there is a “navigation” region that contains links for just that, navigating to different parts of the Surf’s Up web site.</p> <ul> <li>Press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the current page.</li> <li>Press R to move to the different regions on the page. Regions are not visible on the screen, but they are used to make it easy to get from one part of the page to another. The main region is where the main text for the page begins. Regions designate the different broad categories on the page, such as the search region, the banner region, and more.</li> <li>Try pressing INSERT+CTRL+R to open a JAWS list of regions.</li> <li>Use the Surf’s Up link at the top of any of the secondary pages of Surf’s Up to move back to the Surf’s Up home page and try these keystrokes there as well.</li> <li>Press ENTER on the main region in the list. JAWS moves focus directly to that part of the page. Many web sites have a graphic company logo, which is also a link, at the top of their web pages to make it easier for you to get back to their home page. Surf’s Up mimics this behavior so you can practice using it as well. At the top of every page in Surf’s Up besides the home page is a graphic link that simply reads, “Surf’s Up.” It is a small thumbnail image of a shark’s fin which is also a link to the Surf’s Up home page.</li> </ul> <h3 id="navigation-quick-keys-for-jaws">Navigation Quick Keys for JAWS</h3> <h4 id="navigation-quick-keys-for-jaws-1">Navigation Quick Keys for JAWS</h4> <p>Navigation Quick Keys make it faster and easier to move around on a Web page and anywhere else the Virtual Cursor is active. These commands are all assigned to keys on the main part of the keyboard, and are easy to remember and use. Press CTRL+F4 to close this page when you are finished reading it.</p> <p>JAWS Tip: You can use the SHIFT key in combination with many of the keystrokes in the table below to move to the previous unit or element.</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Quick Key</p> <p>Radio Button</p> <p>A</p> <p>Button</p> <p>B</p> <p>Combo Box, List Box, or Tree View</p> <p>C</p> <p>Different Type Element</p> <p>D</p> <p>Edit Box</p> <p>E</p> <p>Form Control</p> <p>F</p> <p>Graphic</p> <p>G</p> <p>Heading</p> <p>H</p> <p>Item in a List</p> <p>I</p> <p>Jump to Line</p> <p>J</p> <p>Return to Previous Line</p> <p>SHIFT+J</p> <p>Jump to Cell (Within Table)</p> <p>CTRL+WINDOWS Key+J or WINDOWS Key+J in Mozilla Firefox</p> <p>Return to Previous Table Cell</p> <p>CTRL+SHIFT+WINDOWS Key+J or SHIFT+WINDOWS Key+J in Mozilla Firefox</p> <p>PlaceMarker</p> <p>K</p> <p>Temporary PlaceMarker</p> <p>WINDOWS Key+CTRL+K</p> <p>Add, Delete, Edit, or Rename Permanent PlaceMarker</p> <p>CTRL+SHIFT+K</p> <p>Speak All PlaceMarkers</p> <p>ALT+WINDOWS Key+K</p> <p>PlaceMarker 1</p> <p>7</p> <p>PlaceMarker 2</p> <p>8</p> <p>PlaceMarker 3</p> <p>9</p> <p>PlaceMarker 4</p> <p>0</p> <p>List</p> <p>L</p> <p>Frame</p> <p>M</p> <p>Non-link Text</p> <p>N</p> <p>Article Region</p> <p>O</p> <p>Paragraph</p> <p>P</p> <p>Move to Main Region of a Page</p> <p>Q</p> <p>Region</p> <p>R</p> <p>Same Type Element</p> <p>S</p> <p>Table</p> <p>T</p> <p>Unvisited Link</p> <p>U</p> <p>Visited Link</p> <p>V</p> <p>Word From List</p> <p>W</p> <p>Check Box</p> <p>X</p> <p>Span</p> <p>Y</p> <p>Division</p> <p>Z</p> <p>Heading at Level</p> <p>1 through 6</p> <p>Separator</p> <p>DASH</p> <p>Clickable Element</p> <p>SLASH</p> <p>Move to OnMouseOver</p> <p>SEMICOLON</p> <p>Tab Control</p> <p>APOSTROPHE</p> <p>Step Past Element</p> <p>SHIFT+PERIOD</p> <p>Step Before Element</p> <p>SHIFT+COMMA</p> <h5 id="html-navigation-quick-keys-for-say-all">HTML Navigation Quick Keys for Say All</h5> <p>Many of the JAWS navigation quick keys are also available while using Say All on a Web page. The commands to move by heading, paragraph, form control, table, list, same or different element, next element, and to move to non-link text all work while you are using the Say All command (INSERT+DOWN ARROW).</p> <h5 id="quick-keys-settings">Quick Keys Settings</h5> <p>Navigation Quick Keys are on by default, but you can turn them off, or set them to work only within Say All. Press INSERT+N (only when using the virtual cursor) to toggle this setting. You can also change this setting for the current web browser in Quick Settings with (INSERT+V), or globally for all programs in JAWS Settings Center. To temporarily suspend the use of Navigation Quick Keys without completely turning them off, press INSERT+SHIFT+Z.</p> <h5 id="navigation-quick-key-manager-1">Navigation Quick Key Manager</h5> <p>Navigation Quick Key manager is used to view, edit, or delete Navigation Quick Key assignments. To open Navigation Quick Key manager do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+J to switch to the JAWS window.</li> <li>From within the JAWS window press ALT+U to open the Utilities menu.</li> <li>Press N to open the Navigation Quick Key manager submenu. Focus moves to the first item of three, HTML/PDF.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move through the other two items. You find one for Microsoft Word and one for Microsoft Outlook. NOTE: You can also find Navigation Quick Key Manager in the list of JAWS managers by pressing INSERT+F2.</li> </ul> <h5 id="lists-of-elements">Lists of Elements</h5> <p>If you hold down CTRL+INSERT before pressing certain navigation quick keys, JAWS displays a list of all elements of that particular type on the page. For example, to display a list of all check boxes on the page, press CTRL+INSERT+X. Use the UP and DOWN ARROW keys to select an item in the list. You can then press ENTER to move to that item’s location on the page.</p> <p>You can use this keystroke to view lists of the following elements: buttons, check boxes, combo boxes, divisions, edit boxes, graphics, lists, radio buttons, tables, and more.</p> <p>Additionally, you can get a list of all Virtual HTML Features on a Web page by pressing INSERT+F3.</p> <p>Remember to press CTRL+F4 to close this page when you are finished reading it.</p> <h3 id="personalized-web-page-settings">Personalized Web Page Settings</h3> <h4 id="personalized-web-page-settings-1">Personalized Web Page Settings</h4> <p>You can configure many JAWS settings for specific Web sites. Personalized settings apply to all pages of a given domain, such as CNN.com or Vispero.com. Some examples where using personalized settings could be useful might include:</p> <ul> <li>Turn off heading announcement on Web sites that use headings to format information rather than structure it.</li> <li>Turn off inline frames on sites that use them for advertising.</li> <li>Turn off announcement of image map links on sites that do not provide alternate text for them, but do provide text links as well.</li> <li>And more… Make the various JAWS settings work for you to enhance your experiences on the Internet.</li> </ul> <p>JAWS includes many configurable settings to access information on Web pages as efficiently as possible, and JAWS uses default settings that provide the most information on the majority of Web sites. However, there are many Web sites that are not designed with accessibility in mind or do not use HTML correctly. When using JAWS default settings, some of these Web pages may not provide enough information, while others may provide too much.</p> <h5 id="what-settings-can-be-personalized">What Settings can be Personalized?</h5> <p>You can personalize many types of Web settings. For example:</p> <ul> <li>Prevent Web sites from automatically refreshing, so the information does not reload and cause JAWS to read from the top of the page all over again.</li> <li>Turn off graphic links on sites where alternate text is not provided or where the graphic links do not provide useful information.</li> <li>Turn off heading announcement when headings are not used to structure information on a page.</li> <li>Turn off navigation quick keys on pages that use certain types of access keys so the keys do not conflict.</li> <li>Personalize Web settings for forms, frames, lists, and long quotations.</li> </ul> <h5 id="personalizing-web-settings">Personalizing Web Settings</h5> <p>Do the following to create or modify personalized settings for a Web page. Note that changes made are saved permanently to JSI files (for example, Vispero.com.jsi) and do not apply to other Web pages. JSI files are stored in the PersonalizedSettings folder, which can be found by opening the Utilities menu from the JAWS window, selecting the Explore Utilities Folder option, and then choosing Explore My Settings.</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+V to open the Quick Settings dialog box. Focus is in the Search edit box.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the Quick Settings tree view.</li> <li>Press P to move to the Personalize Web Settings group. If necessary, press RIGHT ARROW to expand the group.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the different options and groups within Personalize Web Settings, and press SPACEBAR to make changes.</li> <li>After making all necessary changes, press TAB to move to the OK button and then press SPACEBAR to save changes and exit Quick Settings.</li> </ul> <h5 id="sharing-personalized-settings">Sharing Personalized Settings</h5> <p>JAWS stores personalized settings information in JSI files. To share your personalized settings with other JAWS users</p> <ul> <li>From the JAWS application window, press ALT+U to open the Utilities menu and press X to activate the Explore Utilities Folder option.</li> <li>Navigate to Explore My Settings and press ENTER. A folder opens that contains all of the files you have had JAWS modify or create for you.</li> <li>Select the folder PersonalizedSettings and press ENTER to open it.</li> <li>Locate the JSI file with the domain name of the page that uses the personalized settings you want to share. For example: “Google.com.jsi.”</li> <li>Copy this file and distribute it to others. Those you share your JSI file with need to copy the JSI file into their user folder on their computer following the steps above. They can now use that HTML page with your personalized settings.</li> </ul> <h3 id="reading-pages-with-frames">Reading Pages with Frames</h3> <h4 id="reading-pages-with-frames-1">Reading Pages with Frames</h4> <p>Some web pages use frames to display content. A frame is an area of the page that browsers treats like a separate window. Each frame is capable of displaying an independent Web page. The <a href="Frame-Example.htm">Vispero Company Info</a> page is a sample web page that uses frames to display different types of information. One frame contains addresses for Vispero locations, another contains a brief history of the company, and the last frame contains some general information about Vispero.</p> <p>In the following exercises, you will use a sample web page to learn how to navigate frames:</p> <ul> <li>Go to the <a href="Frame-Example.htm">Vispero Company Info</a> sample Web page. Notice that JAWS says there are three frames.</li> <li>When you first open the sample Web page, you are in the Company Locations frame. Press INSERT+F9 to display a list of all the frames on this page.</li> <li>Select “Corporate History” and press ENTER. JAWS moves you to the Corporate History frame.</li> <li>Use the JAWS reading commands to read all the text in this frame. Notice that as you navigate, JAWS does not indicate when you leave the current frame and move into the next frame. This is the default behavior and is explained below.</li> <li>Press M to move to the next frame on the page. Notice that JAWS reads the first line of text in the frame which in this case is a level 1 heading.</li> <li>Press SHIFT+M to move back to the previous frame. By default, JAWS does not announce when you enter or leave a fframe. This is because many frames on websites are not labeled properly and most of the time, a frame’s title does not accurately reflect its content. One example is a Google Maps frame that is used on some websites to show the location of the particular company. Many times, the lable for these frames is just a series of letters and numbers, which provides no useful information when announced by JAWS.</li> </ul> <p>If you would like JAWS to indicate when you enter or leave a frame, do the following:</p> <ul> <li><p>Press INSERT+F2, and select Settings Center.</p></li> <li><p>In the Search edit box, type “web verbosity” without the quotes.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to “Configure Web Verbosity Levels” in the filtered search results in the tree view and press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Press RIGHT ARROW to expand the “Configure Web Verbosity Levels” group.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Medium and press SPACEBAR. A dialog box opens containing a tree view listing the structural elements that can be announced by the Virtual Cursor.</p></li> <li><p>Press F until you reach Frames and press the SPACEBAR to toggle the announcement of this element.</p></li> <li><p>Select OK to exit this dialog box and select OK once more to close Settings Center. Now, to see how this works:</p></li> <li><p>Go to the <a href="Frame-Example.htm">Vispero Company Info</a> sample Web page. JAWS now says “Contact Information Frame” which is the first frame on the page.</p></li> <li><p>Begin using the arrow keys to read the text. As you move through the page, JAWS announces the name of the previous frame and says, “Frame end.” JAWS then announces the name of the next frame.</p></li> <li><p>Press M and SHIFT+M to move between frames. JAWS now speaks the actual name of the frame instead of reading the heading as it did in the previous exercise when frame announcement was disabled.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="inline-frames">Inline Frames</h5> <p>Inline Frames are embedded directly within a Web page and display the contents of another page. Visually, these types of frames usually look like images or banners. Inline frames are often used by Websites to display advertisements. To ignore inline frames use Quick Settings as follows:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+V. Quick Settings opens with focus in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type in inline. The tree view below the edit box changes to filter out results that do not match.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the item Inline Frames Show. The default is On.</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to toggle this setting to Off.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. Quick settings closes and the changes are saved.</li> </ul> <h3 id="sample-news-page">Sample News Page</h3> <p><a href="https://www.vispero.com/">Home</a> <a href="https://www.vispero.com/training">Training</a><a href="https://www.vispero.com/support/support">Documentation</a><a href="https://www.vispero.com/downloads/">Downloads</a><a href="https://www.vispero.com/contact/">Contact Us</a></p> <p>This is a sample news page that has several elements, including links across the top of the page, frames with widgets for social media Web sites, and an advertisement in a division on the page.</p> <h4 id="flexible-web">Flexible Web</h4> <p>Frequently, you will encounter web pages containing a lot of excess content, such as advertisements, which can make it difficult to locate the actual content you want, or interrupts the flow when reading. These can be troublesome for JAWS users as they disrupt the reading order of surrounding content.</p> <p>Flexible Web enables you to take more control of Web pages by allowing you to quickly find the content you are looking for, as well as hide content that interrupts the reading experience. You can hide sections of content, such as frames containing advertisements or other types of unnecessary content, for a smoother reading experience. In addition, you could have JAWS begin reading at a level one heading, or ARIA main region, as these may contain the most interesting content.</p> <p>To use Flexible Web:</p> <ul> <li><p>Open a web page you want to customize in Edge, Chrome, or Firefox.</p></li> <li><p>Then, move the Virtual PC Cursor to the page element you want to hide, or from where you want to start reading when the page first loads.</p></li> <li><p>Activate the Flexible Web wizard by pressing the layered keystroke INSERT+SPACEBAR, followed by X. Alternatively, press INSERT+F2 to open the Run JAWS Manager dialog box, and then choose Flexible Web. Through several easy-to-follow steps, The Flexible Web wizard that opens provides you with two options:</p></li> <li><p>Hide</p></li> <li><p>Start reading at the selected element The wizard then guides you through the process of creating a temporary customization by giving you various choices about the selected element and how you want to hide it or from where exactly to start reading. Once the customization has been made, it is immediately applied to the page. For instance, if you choose to hide all frames containing advertisements, you will not see any advertisements when navigating the page after making this temporary customization.</p></li> </ul> <p>If you are not happy with how a customization is working, you can open the Flexible Web wizard to undo the last customization you made. When you return to the page, you can choose a different element or the same one, and then reactivate the Flexible Web wizard to retry the customization again perhaps with different criteria. For example, in the case of hiding those advertisement frames mentioned earlier, you probably want to hide all of them, not just the first one on the page. The wizard will provide you with choices about whether to hide just the first one or all of them.</p> <p>You can create as many customizations for a page as you want. Once you have created one or more customizations, you can save them as a rule, which is applied every time you load the particular page or site. To indicate that a rule has been applied to a page, JAWS plays a sound after the page loads. Rules can be applied to the current Web page, entire Web site, or globally for all Web sites. Otherwise, customizations are only temporary and are lost as soon as you navigate away from the current Web page or close the browser. If you have made temporary customizations and you attempt to navigate to another page or close the browser, a dialog box opens asking if you want to save your customizations as a rule.</p> <p>To learn more about using Flexible Web, refer to the Flexible Web help topic in the JAWS online help (F1).</p> <h3 id="screen-layout-mode-step-by-step-instructions">Screen layout Mode Step-by-step Instructions</h3> <p>Do the following to enable Screen Layout mode in your web browser:</p> <ul> <li>In the web browser, press INSERT+V. The Quick Settings dialog box opens with focus in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type document presentation in the search edit box. The tree view below filters out everything that does not relate to document presentation.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW until focus moves to Document Presentation Mode.</li> <li>Press the SPACEBAR to choose Screen Layout.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then press SPACEBAR to activate it. NOTE: By default, the quick settings for JAWS are saved to your computer hard disk, and remain set this way until you change them back or to a different setting.</li> </ul> <p>If you determine that Screen Layout mode is better suited to your needs for all programs, you can do the following to permanently enable this feature globally:</p> <ul> <li>In the web browser, press INSERT+F2.</li> <li>Select Settings Center and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+D to switch to the default file.</li> <li>Focus is in the Search edit box. Type in “select layout” without the quotes.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Select Layout in the filtered results of the tree view in Settings Center.</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to toggle from Simple Layout to Screen Layout.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. The changes are made and saved. Settings Center closes. Press CTRL+F4 to close this window when you are finished reading it.</li> </ul> <h3 id="skim-reading">Skim Reading</h3> <h4 id="skim-reading-1">Skim Reading</h4> <p>Skim reading is a powerful reading, searching, and navigation tool available in JAWS. This feature allows you to quickly review long documents by reading the first line or sentence of each paragraph. Alternatively, you can search for passages containing specific words or phrases. In this section, you will learn how to skim read a Web page with JAWS. You will also learn how to create text rules and use them to skim Web pages for specific information.</p> <p>NOTE: Before beginning the first exercise in this section, you should ensure that your skim reading preferences use the default settings. If you have previously changed these settings, press CTRL+SHIFT+INSERT+DOWN ARROW and verify that the Read First Line of Every Paragraph radio button is selected before continuing.</p> <h5 id="skimming-a-document">Skimming a Document</h5> <p>You can skim read a lengthy Web page to get an overview of the content and search for paragraphs or sections containing specific information.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Follow along with the instructions below to practice skim reading text on the Internet with JAWS.</p> <ul> <li><p>Open the sample page <a href="FS-Software.htm">Vispero Software Solutions</a>, and press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</p></li> <li><p>Press CTRL+INSERT+DOWN ARROW to begin skim reading.
