Press CTRL+SHIFT+Y to close the Collections Pane.</li> </ul> <p>Extensions improve the browsing experience by adding or modifying features and functionality to Edge. Examples include ad blockers, password managers, and extensions for popular applications. You can install, manage, and delete them in Edge using the keyboard. To do this:</p> <ul> <li>Press ALT+F to open the Settings and More menu.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to locate Extensions and press ENTER.</li> <li>A modal dialog opens, displaying options for managing Extensions. These include: <ul> <li>Open Microsoft Edge Add-Ons Website</li> <li>Manage Extensions</li> <li>Extensions page</li> <li>More Options</li> </ul></li> <li>Press ENTER or SPACEBAR on these options to activate them.</li> <li>Use the Microsoft Edge Add-Ons website to search for and install extensions and add-ons.</li> <li>Use Manage Extensions and the Extensions button to search for and browse installed extensions.</li> <li>Use the More Options menu to open a context menu that gives you the option of showing the Extensions button in the Edge Toolbar.</li> <li>Press ESC to close the Extensions window and return to the current web page, or press ALT+F4 to close the Edge window. Following are some commonly used shortcut keystrokes for Edge. For a complete list, refer to the <a href="https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/help/4531783/microsoft-edge-keyboard-shortcuts">Edge Keyboard Shortcuts</a> page on the Microsoft website.</li> </ul> <p>Description</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Open a new window</p> <p>CTRL+N</p> <p>Open a new tab</p> <p>CTRL+T</p> <p>Move to next open tab</p> <p>CTRL+TAB</p> <p>Move to previous open tab</p> <p>CTRL+SHIFT+TAB</p> <p>Mute or unmute audio in current tab</p> <p>CTRL+M</p> <p>Close current tab</p> <p>CTRL+F4</p> <p>Close Edge (will close all open tabs)</p> <p>ALT+F4</p> <p>Open Edge main menu</p> <p>ALT+F or ALT+E</p> <p>Move to the Address bar</p> <p>ALT+D</p> <p>Open a web page</p> <p>CTRL+L</p> <p>Open file on local computer</p> <p>CTRL+O</p> <p>Reload the current page</p> <p>F5</p> <p>Add current page to favorites</p> <p>CTRL+D</p> <p>Add favorites for all open tabs in a new folder</p> <p>CTRL+SHIFT+D</p> <p>Open Favorites manager</p> <p>CTRL+SHIFT+O</p> <p>Open history</p> <p>CTRL+H</p> <p>Open list of recently downloaded files</p> <p>CTRL+J</p> <p>Toggle Immersive Reader</p> <p>F9</p> <p>Open Collections pane</p> <p>CTRL+SHIFT+Y</p> <h3 id="using-custom-labels">Using Custom Labels</h3> <h4 id="using-custom-labels-1">Using Custom Labels</h4> <p>The Custom Labels feature is an extremely flexible and versatile way to customize Web pages to suit your individual needs. JAWS allows you to assign custom text labels to almost any HTML element that you can move to by pressing the TAB key. These elements include text links, graphic links, form fields, and buttons. You can also label images on Web pages. JAWS reads these custom labels instead of the identifying text assigned to the elements by the Web page author. JAWS also uses custom labels to identify elements when they appear in lists, such as the list of form fields that displays when you press INSERT+F5.</p> <p>You can use this feature to customize the elements of any Web page to help you navigate the page, reduce verbosity, compensate for incomplete or poorly labeled elements, and similar functions. Redefine the labels for entire Web forms or applications so the names are more useful and meaningful to you. Customize Web pages so that links and graphics provide more information and help you find what you need right away. The Custom Labels feature provides unmatched flexibility in the way you read Web pages.</p> <p>NOTE: JAWS saves the labels you assign to a Web page so they are available each time you use that page. In addition, the labels you create are applied to identical elements any time they appear in that page’s domain. The domain is usually the first part of the page’s Web address. For example, if you assign a label to a button, JAWS reads that label any time you encounter the button on any Web page within that domain. Custom labels are saved in JSI files in the Settingsfolder.</p> <p>The following exercises demonstrate how you can use custom labels to make Web pages easier to use and more informative.</p> <h5 id="labeling-an-image-map">Labeling an Image Map</h5> <p>The image at the very top of the Customer Response Form depicts three tabs that users can click to navigate to other sections of the site. When JAWS reads this image, it says, “Graphic navigation tabs.” This graphic is a special type called an image map. Image maps have one or more areas on them that act like links. Mouse users can click these areas, and JAWS users can press ENTER to activate these links.</p> <p>EXERCISE: The image map on the sample Customer Response Form is not coded to work well with JAWS. In this exercise, you’ll use custom labels to make the image map easier to use:</p> <ul> <li><p>Open the <a href="CustomerResponseForm.htm">Customer Response Form</a> sample Web page.</p></li> <li><p>Press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the page.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW until you hear JAWS announce “image map link tab2.” The information provided by the page author is not very helpful in determining what this link actually does.</p></li> <li><p>Press ENTER to activate the link. The message that displays tells you what this link does. On a real Web page, the link would take you to another page without displaying the message. You would have to explore the site more thoroughly to discover what the link actually does.</p></li> <li><p>After reading the message, press ENTER to close this dialog box. TIP: Normally, if you follow a link to see what it does, you can return to the original page by pressing ALT+LEFT ARROW.</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+F2. Select “Custom Label,” and press ENTER to assign a custom label to this image map link.</p></li> <li><p>Since this link takes you to the Products page, type “Products” and press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to read the next image map link. This link also doesn’t have a good description. Press ENTER to find out what this link does.</p></li> <li><p>After reading the message, press ENTER to close this dialog box.</p></li> <li><p>Next, press INSERT+CTRL+TAB. This keystroke is a shortcut you can use to label an HTML element.</p></li> <li><p>Since this image map link takes you to the Shopping page, type “Shopping,” and press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Press CTRL+HOME and then begin reading the page again. Notice that JAWS now reads the labels you assigned to the image map links instead of “tab2” and “tab3.” JAWS Tip: JAWS also uses the custom label whenever the element appears in an HTML list. Press INSERT+F7. Notice that the labels you created are used to indicate the image map links in the list instead of “tab2” and “tab3.”</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="labeling-a-text-link">Labeling a Text Link</h5> <p>Often times, the actual text of a link will not be very descriptive. You can use custom labels to change the text of a link. Use this feature to shorten wordy links or add more description to short links.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Follow along with the steps below to see how you can use JAWS to label text links.</p> <ul> <li>Open the <a href="CustomerResponseForm.htm">Customer Response Form</a> sample Web page.</li> <li>Press INSERT+F7 to display a list of links on the page. Find the link named “click here.” That name isn’t very descriptive. Select the link “click here” and choose Move to Link to go to the link’s location on the page so you can find out more about it.</li> <li>Press ALT+NUM PAD 5 to read the sentence this link appears in. From the context of the sentence, you can determine that the link allows you to send e-mail to the Webmaster.</li> <li>Press INSERT+CTRL+TAB to label this link.</li> <li>Type “Send the Webmaster e-mail” without the quotes, and then press ENTER.</li> <li>Press ALT+NUM PAD 5 to read the sentence again. Notice that JAWS reads your label instead of the words “click here.”</li> <li>Press INSERT+F7 again. The entry “click here” that was previously in the list has been replaced by “Send the Webmaster e-mail.” Any time you assign a custom label, JAWS displays that label when the element appears in HTML lists.</li> <li>Press ESC to close the list of links when you are finished.</li> </ul> <h5 id="labeling-form-fields">Labeling Form Fields</h5> <p>You can also assign custom labels to form fields and controls, such as edit boxes, radio buttons, combo boxes, check boxes, and buttons.</p> <p>EXERCISE: In this exercise you’ll assign custom labels to some unlabeled edit fields.</p> <ul> <li>Open the <a href="CustomerResponseForm.htm">Customer Response Form</a> sample Web page.</li> <li>Press F to move to the first form field on the page. This form is poorly designed. Most of the fields are labeled incorrectly or aren’t labeled at all. Press INSERT+F5 to display a list of form fields. You can see that the majority of fields in this list are unlabeled.</li> <li>Press E several times to move through the first three edit boxes on the page. JAWS announces the label for the first field as “full name” but the next two edit fields have no label. In reality, the first field should be labeled “first name,” the second field should be labeled “middle initial,” and the third field should be labeled “last name.”</li> <li>Press SHIFT+E twice to return to the first edit box, and then press INSERT+CTRL+TAB.</li> <li>Type “First Name” and press ENTER to label this field. Assign meaningful labels to the other two edit boxes using the Custom Label command (INSERT+CTRL+TAB).</li> <li>Press F until you hear, “Address.” Press the TAB key four times and listen to JAWS announce each address-related field. See if you can determine the purpose of each field and then assign each a meaningful custom label.</li> <li>When you’ve finished, press X. This command moves you to the first of three check boxes that you can use to indicate your level of customer satisfaction. Each check box is labeled with an image (a happy face, an indifferent face, and an angry face). Though the descriptions you hear for the check boxes are long, they are accurate and coded correctly. These particular descriptions come from the images’ ALT text. In this case, the Web author primarily intended to use this ALT text to provide further information to sighted users when they move the mouse pointer over the image.</li> <li>Use custom labels to shorten these verbose labels. Press INSERT+CTRL+TAB, type “Good,” and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press X to move to the next check box and give it the label “Fair.” Then press X again and label the last check box “Poor.”</li> <li>Press E to move to an unlabeled multiline edit box. From the introductory paragraph and the initial text, you can deduce that this area is where you enter your comments. Press INSERT+CTRL+TAB, type “Comments,” and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press INSERT+F5 to review all of the form fields on this page. JAWS displays all the fields using the custom labels you assigned to them. This form should be much easier to fill out now. Go ahead and fill out the form to see how you’ve used custom labels to greatly enhance its usability.</li> </ul> <h5 id="sharing-custom-labels">Sharing Custom Labels</h5> <p>After you assign some custom labels to a page, you can share those labels with other users. Custom labels are saved in JSI files, just like personalized Web settings. To share your custom labels with other JAWS users</p> <ul> <li>From the JAWS application window, press ALT+U to open the Utilities menu and press X to activate the Explore Utilities Folder option.</li> <li>Navigate to Explore My Settings and press ENTER. A folder opens that contains all of the files you have had JAWS modify or create for you.</li> <li>Select the folder PersonalizedSettings and press ENTER to open it.</li> <li>Locate the JSI file with the domain name of the page that contains the custom labels you want to share. For example: “Google.com.jsi.”</li> <li>Copy this file and distribute it to others. Those you share your JSI file with need to copy the JSI file into their user folder on their computer following the steps above. They can now use that HTML page with your custom labels.</li> </ul> <h5 id="deleting-custom-labels">Deleting Custom Labels</h5> <p>You can delete specific custom labels at any time, or you can delete all custom labels on a page. To delete an element’s label, move to it with standard JAWS reading commands, the TAB key, a Navigation Quick Key, or a JAWS HTML list. Then, press INSERT+F2, select “Custom Label Delete,” and press ENTER. JAWS will now read the original identifying text instead of your custom label.</p> <p>To delete all custom labels on the current page, press INSERT+F2, select “Custom Label Delete All,” and press ENTER.</p> <h3 id="using-forms-with-jaws">Using Forms with JAWS</h3> <h4 id="using-forms-with-jaws-1">Using Forms with JAWS</h4> <p>HTML forms allow you to access shopping carts, search engines, web-based email, online forums, and more. Forms include controls such as edit boxes, check boxes, radio buttons, combo boxes, and other controls similar to those used in dialog boxes.</p> <p>JAWS takes advantage of the features of HTML used to create forms and allows you to access all kinds of form controls.</p> <h5 id="moving-through-forms">Moving Through Forms</h5> <p>The following is a list of JAWS navigation quick key commands that allow you to move quickly from one control to another. You can use the SHIFT key in combination with many of the keystrokes to move to the previous unit or element.</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Button</p> <p>B</p> <p>Combo Box</p> <p>C</p> <p>Edit Box</p> <p>E</p> <p>Form Control (generic)</p> <p>F</p> <p>Radio Button</p> <p>A</p> <p>Check Box</p> <p>X</p> <p>First Form Control on a Page</p> <p>INSERT+CTRL+HOME</p> <p>Last Form Control on a Page</p> <p>INSERT+CTRL+END</p> <p>NOTE: These commands do not work in forms mode.</p> <p>You can also display lists of specific types of form controls. To do this, hold down INSERT+CTRL and press one of the navigation quick keys for moving through forms. For example, to view a list of all edit boxes on the page, press INSERT+CTRL+E.</p> <p>To quickly locate a specific form control press INSERT+F5. This command lists all form controls and their contents on the current page. Move through the list and press ENTER to move to the selected control. Forms mode is automatically enabled so you are ready to make changes to the control. And if you have already entered information in a long form, use the Forms List to quickly review the information.</p> <p>TIP: Forms mode is automatically turned off when you activate a button that submits a form.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and press INSERT+F5 to list all the form controls, and experience how easy it is to review the information. Try pressing ENTER from the list of form controls to go into forms mode and edit the form. Press NUM PAD PLUS, or click outside the form fields if you are using a mouse, to get out of forms mode.</p> <h5 id="auto-forms-mode-and-form-controls">Auto Forms Mode and Form Controls</h5> <p>When you use the ARROW keys or press TAB or SHIFT+TAB on a web page and land in an edit field or combo box, forms mode is automatically on. JAWS also plays a sound to confirm that you are in Forms Mode. This is known as Auto Forms Mode and is useful because you never have to remember to manually turn on Forms Mode using the ENTER key when you move to a form control such as an edit field. Additionally, if someone clicks into an edit box with a MOUSE Click, forms mode comes on automatically.</p> <h6 id="sounds-indicating-forms-mode-on-or-off">Sounds Indicating Forms Mode On or Off</h6> <p>You hear one sound when JAWS enters forms mode and a slightly different sound when JAWS exits forms mode. These sounds can be changed to different sounds if you prefer. Here’s how:</p> <ul> <li><p>In your default web browser, press INSERT+F2.</p></li> <li><p>Select Settings Center and press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Focus is in the Search edit box. Type in “select sound for” without the quotes. JAWS filters out all results that do not match the search in the tree view below.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Select Sound for Entering Forms Mode in the filtered results of the tree view in Settings Center.</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR. A dialog box of sound choices opens.</p></li> <li><p>Press UP or DOWN ARROW to move through the list of sounds. JAWS has over 180 sounds included that you can choose from. You can also use first letter navigation.</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR or ALT+P to hear a sample of the sound.</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the OK button when you find a sound you want to use, and press SPACEBAR to activate it. Focus returns to the Settings Center tree view.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Select Sound for Leaving Forms Mode in the filtered results of the tree view in Settings Center.</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR. A dialog box of sound choices opens.</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR or ALT+P to hear a sample of the sound.</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the OK button and activate it with the SPACEBAR. The changes are made and saved. Settings Center closes. Additionally, you can turn the sounds that indicate forms mode on or off by using the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box. Don’t follow these instructions at the moment, since we’ll be using the sounds for the exercises that follow. However, here is how to change it later if you need to:</p></li> <li><p>Press INSERT+V to open the Quick Settings dialog box. Focus is in the search edit box.</p></li> <li><p>Type in “use sound” without the quotes. JAWS filters out all results that do not match the search in the tree view below.</p></li> <li><p>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the item in the tree view “Use Sound - checked” in the Virtual Cursor Options.</p></li> <li><p>Press SPACEBAR to uncheck the check box.</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. Quick Settings closes and the changes are saved. When you exit the form control, either using the arrow keys, the tab key, or by clicking somewhere else outside of the form controls with a mouse, forms mode is turned off and you hear the sound indicating this. Forms mode is also automatically turned off when the form is submitted or the page refreshes. Alternatively, press NUM PAD PLUS at any time to get out of forms mode.</p></li> </ul> <p>When you use JAWS on the Internet, JAWS uses the virtual cursor, an invisible reading cursor, as the default cursor for reading information. As you navigate, there is a visible reading highlight that surrounds the word or line where you are reading, which makes it easier to tell where the virtual cursor is. To complete a form on a web page, you need to use the PC cursor, which is a visible blinking cursor.</p> <p>NOTE: When using JAWS navigation quick keys, the default setting is for forms mode not to come on automatically. This can be changed in the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box accessed by pressing INSERT+V or in the JAWS Settings Center discussed earlier. Using navigation quick keys in forms is discussed in more detail later in this lesson.</p> <h5 id="keyboard-navigation-within-forms">Keyboard Navigation within Forms</h5> <p>Keyboard navigation within forms can be done in many different ways. Most people will use one or a combination of the following:</p> <ul> <li>ARROW keys</li> <li>TAB key</li> <li>Navigation Quick Keys</li> </ul> <h6 id="using-the-arrow-keys-to-explore-a-form">Using the Arrow Keys to Explore a Form</h6> <p>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below and use just the ARROW Keys to explore the form:</p> <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Let’s explore how using the arrow keys works when a form control is encountered. Begin pressing DOWN ARROW one line at a time. Stop when you reach the first field label, First <em>. Just after the label for First </em> is an edit box.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW one time and listen. Did you hear JAWS announce “edit” and play a sound? The sound indicates that forms mode has come on automatically. JAWS announced that the cursor is now in the edit box. You could begin typing now and put your name here, but for now do not do that.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW again. Did you hear a different sound? Forms mode is now off again since the virtual cursor moved out of the edit box and back into the main part of the web page.</li> <li>Continue to press DOWN ARROW to move through the fields for Middle and Last edit boxes. Notice that as you move into an edit box with an arrow key, forms mode comes on automatically and you hear the sound indicating this has happened. Also, as you move out of an edit field with an arrow key, forms mode goes off automatically, and again you hear the sound indicating this has happened. Notice that as you use the arrow keys with JAWS, forms mode only comes on when you are in an edit box. Whenever an edit area is detected, JAWS allows you to begin typing immediately. Yet, at the same time, if focus is not in an edit area, reading mode stays on. This gives you the ability to quickly type information into edit boxes, and still gives you plenty of flexibility to move around the form.</li> </ul> <p>TIP: Why is forms mode not turned on when buttons, check boxes, or other controls are encountered? The reason is because these controls can generally be activated without going into forms mode. For example, the SPACEBAR toggles the check mark on or off for check boxes. Pressing SPACEBAR also moves the selection of a radio button from one choice to another, and activates buttons such as the OK, Cancel, or Submit button. You don’t have to switch to forms mode to do this.</p> <h6 id="using-the-tab-key-to-explore-a-form">Using the TAB Key to Explore a Form</h6> <p>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below and use only the TAB key to move through the form:</p> <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Press the navigation quick key F to move to the first field on the page, the First * edit box.</li> <li>Remember, forms mode does NOT come on automatically when using navigation quick keys. Press ENTER to go into forms mode.</li> <li>Go ahead and type your first name here if you have not already done so. Did you hear JAWS announce that this is a required field? Often, web page developers use the asterisk, *, to indicate required fields. The asterisk can be seen by sighted individuals and you can hear it with JAWS when reading through the form with the arrow keys. The text that JAWS spoke, First Name, this is a required field, is delivered by an ARIA attribute called aria-label. In this case the aria-label gives information that is not visible on the screen such as the word, “Name” and the phrase, “This is a required field.” ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications, and is a technical specification for increasing the accessibility of web pages.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the next edit field, Middle. Did you hear JAWS announce, “Middle initial?” In this case the web page author used a different HTML attribute, the title attribute, to give you the extra information. The word “initial” is not visible on the screen. It is, however, shown as a visible tool tip to people who hover a mouse over the field.</li> <li>Press TAB again to move to the Last * field. Again, you should hear JAWS announce, “Last name. This is a required field,” as a result of the aria-label attribute. As you continue to press TAB or SHIFT+TAB notice that as long as you are in an edit box, forms mode is turned on automatically. When the cursor moves out of an edit box, forms mode goes off automatically, and you hear the sound indicating this has happened.</li> </ul> <h6 id="forms-that-automatically-advance-to-the-next-field">Forms that Automatically Advance to the Next Field</h6> <p>Web page authors may sometimes create form fields that move the PC cursor to the next form field automatically. This can make a long day of filling out forms a lot easier! These types of form controls that automatically move the cursor to the next field are typically seen in fields that have a fixed number of characters, such as phone number fields and social security number fields. As soon as the final character is input, the form moves the cursor immediately to the next field or control.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Follow along and experience how some form fields can advance the cursor to the next field automatically when the first field is complete:</p> <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Press TAB several times to move to the Area Code edit box. This is the first of three telephone number edit boxes.</li> <li>In this first one, type in three numbers. The focus automatically moves to the next field.</li> <li>In the second phone number field, the Exchange edit box, type in another three numbers. The focus automatically moves to the next field, the four digit phone number edit box.</li> <li>In the Number edit box, type in four numbers. Notice that the focus automatically moves to the next field, the email address field. NOTE: The Web Track sample form used in Surf’s Up does not collect or send any data. It is just a practice page.</li> </ul> <p>You will occasionally come across similar types of auto-advance edit fields as you interact with forms on the web.</p> <h6 id="autocomplete-settings">AutoComplete Settings</h6> <p>Most web browsers offer an AutoComplete feature to help you remember things you type. This can happen when typing in edit boxes for web page addresses, search inquiries, and more. This option is enabled by default in Edge, Chrome, and Firefox. If you are in an edit field where you have typed some information previously, as you type, a list forms near the edit field containing a match of any words beginning with the letters you type. You can then choose a word or phrase from the list and press TAB to move to the next form control without having to retype the whole word or phrase.</p> <p>If you choose to keep the AutoComplete Settings on, if you press UP or DOWN ARROW you may find that the focus goes into a list of items that you have typed at some point in the past. This is designed to make it easier for you when filling out forms. It keeps you from having to retype a lot of information. To get out of such an edit box list of choices, perform the following two steps:</p> <ul> <li>First, press ESC to close the list.</li> <li>Then press NUM PAD PLUS to turn forms mode off again. Now you can continue to use the arrow keys to explore and read through the form.</li> </ul> <p>If you prefer not to have your browser display a list of possible choices when typing in form fields, you can turn this feature off. Press ENTER on one of the following links to view information on changing autocomplete settings for your specific browser. After pressing ENTER, press DOWN ARROW to review the information.</p> <p><a href="javascript:unhide('ChangeEdge');">Turning Off (or On) the AutoComplete Settings in Edge</a></p> <h6 id="turning-off-or-on-the-autocomplete-settings-in-edge">Turning Off (or On) the AutoComplete Settings in Edge</h6> <ul> <li>Press ALT+F to open the Settings and more menu and press S to open the Settings page. If Forms mode is activated, press ESC to turn it off.</li> <li>When the settings open, the Profiles page is currently active. Press B to move to the Personal info button and press ENTER.</li> <li>There are two check boxes on this page: Save and fill basic info and Save and fill custom info. Use the SPACEBAR to clear one or both of these check boxes.</li> <li>Press CTRL+F4 to close the Settings page and your changes are automatically saved. <a href="javascript:unhide('ChangeChrome');">Turning Off (or On) the AutoComplete Settings in Chrome</a></li> </ul> <h6 id="turning-off-or-on-the-autocomplete-settings-in-chrome">Turning Off (or On) the AutoComplete Settings in Chrome</h6> <ul> <li>Press ALT+F to open the Chrome menu and press S to open the Settings page. Focus is placed in the Search edit box.</li> <li>Note: You may need to press ENTER to turn on Forms mode if it did not automatically activate. <ul> <li>Press TAB to move to the menu listing the different settings categories.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Autofill and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the Addresses and more link and press ENTER.</li> <li>Move to the Addresses and more button.</li> <li>This is a toggle button. If you hear JAWS say “pressed” after announcing the button name, this means the option is enabled. Press ENTER to toggle this setting.</li> <li>Press CTRL+F4 to close the Settings page.</li> </ul></li> <li><a href="javascript:unhide('ChangeFirefox');">Turning Off (or On) the AutoComplete Settings in Firefox</a></li> </ul> <h6 id="turning-off-or-on-the-autocomplete-settings-in-firefox">Turning Off (or On) the AutoComplete Settings in Firefox</h6> <pre><code>- Press ALT+T to open the Tools menu and press S to open the Settings page. - Press SHIFT+TAB to move to the list of categories.</code></pre> <ul> <li>Note: You may need to press ENTER to turn on Forms mode if it did not automatically activate. <ul> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to select Privacy and security and press ESC to turn off Forms mode.</li> <li>Press C to move to the Firefox will combo box under the History heading and press ENTER to activate Forms mode.</li> <li>Press U to select “Use custom settings for history.”</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the Remember form and search history check box and press SPACEBAR to clear this option.</li> <li>Press CTRL+F4 to close the Settings page and your changes are automatically saved.</li> </ul></li> </ul> <h6 id="navigation-quick-keys-in-forms-with-auto-forms-mode-off-default-setting">Navigation Quick Keys in Forms with Auto Forms Mode off (Default Setting)</h6> <ul> <li>When using navigation quick keys in forms, forms mode does not turn on automatically. This is great because it gives you the ability to move quickly from one part of a form to another without having to worry about forms mode coming on.</li> <li>For example, let’s say you have an email program which is web-based. Often there will be a check box in front of each new item in the Inbox. You can quickly move to a check box by pressing the letter X and then read the subject line of that message. However, you may not want to go into forms mode because you want to move to a Reply button. If forms mode came on when you moved to the check box you would have to turn off forms mode before you could use the navigation quick key B to move to the Reply button.</li> <li>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below to experiment with navigation quick keys: <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Press the navigation quick key B several times to explore what buttons are available in this form. You should find a total of five different buttons. This is a nice way to find out if there is a Submit button or a Send button, for example.</li> <li>Press the navigation quick key A to explore the radio buttons in the form.</li> <li>Next, press the navigation quick key X to explore the check boxes in the form. The check boxes are located in two different areas on this form.</li> <li>Let’s say you have explored the form and now want to move back to the edit box for the first name, which is located near the top of the form. Just press the navigation quick key E and focus wraps back to the top of the page where the first name edit box is located.</li> </ul></li> <li>You can tell from this example how nice it is to be able to use navigation quick keys to explore a form without having forms mode come on. It is also great to be able to move directly and efficiently to certain controls within a form.</li> <li>NOTE: The default setting for JAWS is to NOT go into forms mode when using navigation quick keys. However, this can be changed. Read the next section to find out how.</li> </ul> <h6 id="navigation-quick-keys-in-forms-with-auto-forms-mode-on">Navigation Quick Keys in Forms with Auto Forms Mode On</h6> <ul> <li>If you use forms a lot, you may want to have forms mode come on when using navigation quick keys. You can change JAWS to have forms mode come on if you are using navigation quick keys, and pause for a given number of seconds on a control.</li> <li>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below to experiment with navigation quick keys set to turn on forms mode after pausing for several seconds on a control: <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Open the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box by pressing INSERT+V. Focus is in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type in “delay” without the quotes. JAWS filters out all results that do not match the search in the tree view below.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the item “Navigation Quick Key Delay - Never” in the Virtual Cursor Options.</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to change this to three seconds.</li> <li>Next, press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR. JAWS Quick Settings closes and the changes are saved.</li> </ul></li> <li>Now when using auto forms mode, and navigating with navigation quick keys, JAWS will toggle Forms Mode on after three seconds if you remain on that control. This only happens when the control is an edit box, list, or a combo box. Do you remember why forms mode does not come on for check boxes or buttons? It is because their state can be changed or activated by using the SPACEBAR. <ul> <li>Now, press the navigation quick key E to move through the edit boxes of the form. Make sure to press it within less than three seconds to confirm that you can still navigate without going into forms mode. If you need to change the delay to a little longer, you can adjust the time in the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box up to a maximum of five seconds.</li> <li>Next, press the navigation quick key E again until you find the first name edit box. This time, wait for three seconds. Did you hear the sound indicating that forms mode is now on after the delay?</li> <li>Press NUM PAD PLUS to get out of forms mode for now. You hear the sound indicating that forms mode is now off.</li> </ul></li> <li>You can see how this could be handy for people who fill out forms a lot! For now, go ahead and change the settings back to Navigation Quick Key Delay - Never using the instructions given in steps one through six above.</li> <li>TIP: If you go to a particular domain, such as an Intranet or a group of web pages such as Microsoft.com or Vispero.com where you want this to happen all the time you can use Personalized Settings for JAWS to turn forms mode on when using navigation quick keys every time you visit that site. Personalized Settings can be found in the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box below the section for Virtual Cursor Options.</li> </ul> <h6 id="check-boxes-and-radio-buttons">Check Boxes and Radio Buttons</h6> <ul> <li>To quickly select a check box or radio button on a form, press NUM PAD SLASH when the virtual cursor is on the item. If the selected control is a check box, the state of the check box is toggled. If the control is a radio button that is not selected, this command selects the radio button. JAWS does not switch to forms mode, so you can easily continue reading the page. You can also use SPACEBAR to toggle the state of a check box or select a radio button without going into forms mode.</li> <li>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below to experiment with check boxes and radio buttons: <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Press the navigation quick key A to move to the first group of radio buttons. You hear, “Product(s) in Warranty, Yes radio button checked, one of two.”</li> </ul></li> <li>NOTE: You may not hear the label spoken properly in Chrome or Edge Chromium at the present time. Whenever you hear something that is not expected, don’t hesitate to try the same page in a different browser, such as Firefox. In Firefox the label is currently spoken properly. <ul> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the second radio button. You hear, “radio button not checked.”</li> <li>Press either the keyboard command for the left mouse button, NUM PAD SLASH, or the SPACEBAR to move the check mark from the first radio button to the second one. If you are using a mouse, just click the second radio button.</li> <li>Press UP ARROW to move back to the first radio button and verify it is not checked.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move back to the second radio button and verify it is checked.</li> </ul></li> <li>Notice that throughout the above process, forms mode was never turned on. You used the navigation quick key A for radio buttons to move the virtual cursor to a radio button, and changed the check mark without getting into forms mode.</li> </ul> <h6 id="combo-boxes">Combo Boxes</h6> <ul> <li>When reading with the arrow keys, if the virtual cursor moves to a combo box forms mode is not automatically turned on. (NOTE: Forms mode may come on even when navigating with the virtual cursor if AutoComplete settings are used in that control.) To change the selection, press ALT+DOWN ARROW to open the list of choices. Forms mode comes on. Then, use the ARROW Keys to select an item. Press ALT+UP ARROW to close the list of choices. The item is now selected in the combo box and forms mode goes off again. Then press TAB to move to the next control. (Or use the ARROW KEYS to continue reading.)</li> <li>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below to experiment with combo boxes: <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Press C to move to the combo box for Action Taken.</li> <li>Press UP ARROW to move to the form label, which is to the left of the combo box visually, but on the line above the combo box in the virtual world. You should hear JAWS say “action taken.”</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move back to the combo box.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW again to move below the combo box.</li> </ul></li> <li>Notice that all this time, forms mode has not come on. You are still reading with the virtual cursor. <ul> <li>Press UP ARROW to move back up to the combo box.</li> <li>Press ENTER to go into forms mode. Did you hear the sound indicating that JAWS is now in forms mode? At this point press the ARROW Keys and explore the choices available in the list of items within the combo box.</li> </ul></li> <li>NOTE: Going into a combo box using this method causes only the selected item in the list to be visible within the combo box. Visually, the rest of the list of choices cannot be seen. <ul> <li>Press NUM PAD PLUS to get out of forms mode.</li> <li>Now, try doing it a different way. Still with the virtual cursor on the combo box, press ALT+DOWN ARROW. Did you hear forms mode come on again? Now the list of items in the combo box has been opened so that all items are shown visually. Use the ARROW Keys again to move up and down the list to select a choice.</li> <li>When you have made a selection you want to keep, press ALT+UP ARROW. This action does two things. First, it closes the list with the item you had chosen in the list now visible as the selected choice in the combo box. It also turns forms mode off. Again, you hear the sound indicating that forms mode is off.</li> </ul></li> <li>Spend a few minutes on this combo box practicing the two methods discussed to get into and out of forms mode, and make a selection from the list of available items. When you are finished, make sure that forms mode is off by pressing NUM PAD PLUS.</li> </ul> <h6 id="multiple-selection-list-boxes">Multiple Selection List Boxes</h6> <ul> <li>A variation of a combo box, a multiple selection list box, sometimes called an extended selection list box, can be thought of as a combo box that allows multiple selections. In the combo box example above, only one item can be chosen in the list of values. In a multiple selection list box, more than one item can be chosen in the list of values at one time.</li> <li>If you use a mouse, you can hold down the CTRL key and click any number of items in a multiple selection list. From the keyboard, hold down the CTRL key while moving through the list using UP and DOWN ARROW and press SPACEBAR on the items you want to select. To unselect a previously selected item, press SPACEBAR again on the item.</li> <li>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">New WebTrack Sample Form</a>. Spend a few minutes practicing how to select more than one item at a time in the multiple selection list box on the New WebTrack form. <ul> <li>First, press CTRL+HOME to move to the top of the form.</li> <li>Press the navigation quick key C to move to the multiple selection list box labeled Customer Inquiry. Notice that forms mode did not come on. That is expected behavior. If you did want to go into forms mode at this point, you could press ENTER, but don’t do that right now.</li> <li>Press UP ARROW to move out of the list box and read the label, Customer Inquiry. It is above the list box.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move back down to the list box.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW again to move one line below the list box. You should hear label for the next item, Notes.</li> </ul></li> <li>Notice that you did not go into forms mode by just reading the form with the virtual cursor and the arrow keys. <ul> <li>Now, press CTRL+HOME to move back to the top of the form.</li> <li>Press TAB to move through the form until you reach the Customer Inquiry extended select list box. Notice that as you move through the form, Forms Mode turns on and off automatically as you move past various elements and sounds are played to indicate this has happened.</li> <li>Once in the Customer Inquiry list box, if you just press the ARROW Keys to move up and down the list, only one item is selected. If you press TAB to move out of the control, the last item highlighted in the list will be the only one selected. For now, stay in the list box and move on to the next step.</li> <li>Press and hold the CTRL key and then use UP or DOWN ARROW to navigate the list. For any unselected items in the list, you should hear JAWS say “not selected” followed by the item name.</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to select any item.</li> <li>Continue holding the CTRL key and press DOWN ARROW to move to the next item below the one you selected. Did you hear JAWS announce the item is not selected?</li> <li>Continue holding the CTRL key and press DOWN ARROW again. Did you hear JAWS announce that this item also is not selected?</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to select a second item.</li> <li>Continue to select or unselect as many items in the list as you wish by using the SPACEBAR. You can move up and down the list with the ARROW Keys while still holding down the CTRL key to verify which ones are selected.</li> <li>When you are finished making selections, press TAB to move out of the multiple selection list box to the next field. The items you selected are still highlighted in the multiple selection list box.</li> </ul></li> <li>NOTE: You can also press NUM PAD PLUS or CLICK with a mouse elsewhere in the page outside of a form control to exit forms mode when in a multiple selection list box.</li> </ul> <h5 id="semi-auto-forms-mode">Semi-Auto Forms Mode</h5> <ul> <li>Some options for forms mode can be changed. For example, you might prefer to use the classic forms mode (forms mode off) instead of auto forms mode. Or you may want to use Semi-Auto forms mode. Let us take a look at the Semi-Auto forms mode using JAWS Quick Settings.</li> <li>You can make some adjustments to forms mode by using the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box. JAWS automatically saves the changes you make until you change them again.</li> <li>EXERCISE: Open the <a href="WebTrack.htm">Web Track Sample Form</a> and follow along with the instructions below and explore some of the items you can change in the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box: <ul> <li>First, make sure the cursor is at the top of the page. Press CTRL+HOME.</li> <li>Press INSERT+V to open the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box. Focus is in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type in “auto” without the quotes. JAWS filters out all results that do not match the search in the tree view below.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the choice that reads “Auto Forms Mode - Auto” in the Virtual Cursor Options. There are three options here, Auto, Semi-auto, and Manual.</li> <li>Press SPACEBAR to change this to Semi-auto.</li> <li>Next, press TAB to move to the OK button, and then press SPACEBAR to activate it. Quick Settings closes and the changes are saved. Focus returns to the Web Track sample page.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move through the controls on the page. The virtual cursor finds the label, First *.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the edit box. Notice that forms mode has not come on automatically.</li> <li>Continue to press DOWN ARROW to move through the controls on the page. The virtual cursor reads the label first and then the edit box second for each control. Notice that you do not hear the different sounds indicating forms mode is on, then off, and then on again constantly as you arrow through the form. This is great for people who have to use forms all day long and who have been listening to the different sounds as JAWS goes into and out of forms mode. Much less of a distraction!</li> <li>Now, press TAB and SHIFT+TAB to navigate through the controls on this page. Notice that when you encounter edit fields or combo boxes, Forms Mode automatically turns on and off.</li> <li>When you do come across an edit box using the ARROW keys that you need to enter text in, just press ENTER to go into forms mode.</li> <li>Press NUM PAD PLUS to get out of forms mode when you are finished or press TAB to move to the next form control.</li> </ul></li> <li>We think once you get accustomed to using semi-auto forms mode you will like it very much. Go ahead and follow the instructions above if you wish to switch auto forms mode back on again. When you find the selection that says “Auto Forms Mode - Semi-Auto” just press SPACEBAR to change it back to “Auto” again. Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR.</li> </ul> <h5 id="form-control-prompts">Form Control Prompts</h5> <ul> <li>HTML allows the author of a web page to specifically associate text prompts (or labels) with form controls. JAWS recognizes when a prompt is specifically associated with a control, and speaks the correct prompt when you move to that control. If no prompt is specifically associated with a control, JAWS attempts to identify text positioned near the control as the prompt. This is most accurate when the text is directly to the left or above the form control.</li> </ul> <h5 id="pdf-form">PDF Form</h5> <ul> <li>EXERCISE: Open the attached <a href="ProductInformationRequest.zip">PDF sample form</a> and try it using the techniques you have learned. JAWS handles PDF forms the same way as HTML forms.</li> </ul> <h5 id="list-of-virtual-html-features">List of Virtual HTML Features</h5> <ul> <li>Take a minute to look at and use the JAWS List of Virtual HTML Features, INSERT+F3. This is a handy way to generate lists of many items found in the virtual environment.</li> </ul> <h3 id="using-html-help-systems">Using HTML Help Systems</h3> <h4 id="using-html-help-systems-1">Using HTML Help Systems</h4> <p>Help information for software is often presented in HTML format. You can read and navigate these Help systems just like Web sites on the Internet. A type of help system called HTML Help is used in many different kinds of programs, including JAWS. In addition to presenting information as HTML pages, an HTML Help system can also have an index, full text search capability, glossary, table of contents, and other features. In this section, you will learn how to use the comprehensive search and navigation features of HTML Help systems.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-3">Table of Contents</h5> <p>The table of contents is one of the best ways to browse the various subject matter contained in the Help system. A table of contents contains one or more books. Books contain several related topics.</p> <p>EXERCISE: In the exercise below, you will use the JAWS Help system to learn how to navigate the table of contents.</p> <ul> <li>In the JAWS window, open the Help menu and choose Help Topics. Alternatively, just press F1 from within the JAWS window.</li> <li>Hold CTRL and press the TAB key until you hear “Table of Contents page.” Notice that in the JAWS help there are four tabs in this pane: Table of Contents, Index, Search, and Favorites.</li> <li>Use the UP and DOWN ARROW keys to explore the table of contents. As you move through the table of contents, you are moving through books or topics in a tree view. If a book is closed, you cannot see what topics it contains.</li> <li>Select the book Using the Internet with JAWS, and then press RIGHT ARROW to open it.</li> <li>Use the DOWN ARROW key to explore the topics contained in the book you just opened. Sometimes, in addition to several topics, books can contain other books. When you press down arrow the first time you hear JAWS say, “Level one.” If you continue to press DOWN ARROW you will eventually hear JAWS say “Level zero” and the name of the next book below in the tree, which is closed. Level zero is the top level. As you open and close books and topics, JAWS announces when you change levels. As long as the level does not change when moving up or down, you do not hear the level repeated.</li> <li>Select the book Navigating Web Pages, and press RIGHT ARROW to open it.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to the next level. JAWS tells you that you have moved to level two. You can think of these different levels as having a type of outline structure. Continue to press UP or DOWN ARROW until you select the topic Navigation Quick Keys.</li> <li>Press ENTER to open this topic. The information it contains is displayed in the topic pane on the right side of the window.</li> <li>Press F6 to switch to the topic pane. JAWS automatically begins reading the text in the topic pane. You can use the standard JAWS reading and navigation commands to read this topic. You can use any command or feature that you can use normally with JAWS in a web browser, such as pressing INSERT+F7 to view a list of links, or H to move from one heading to another.</li> <li>When you are finished reading you can press F6 again to move back to the tree view of books and topics. F6 is a command that switches between the two panes of the help window.</li> </ul> <h5 id="index-1">Index</h5> <p>The index of an HTML Help system lets you search by keyword. Indexes are useful for finding specific information about certain subjects.</p> <p>EXERCISE: In this exercise you will use the JAWS help system to learn how to find information in an index.</p> <ul> <li>In JAWS, open the Help menu and choose Help Topics. Alternatively, just press F1 from within the JAWS window.</li> <li>If you are continuing from the previous exercise, first make sure that focus is back in the tree view of books and topics. If you are not certain, press F6 until you hear JAWS announce the tree view.</li> <li>Hold CTRL and press the TAB key until you move to the Index tab page.</li> <li>Let’s assume you want to look up information about how to work with graphics. Type the word graphic.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the list of indexed keywords. The JAWS Help system has selected the closest matching keyword, which is “Graphic Label.” This isn’t the keyword you are looking for.</li> <li>Use the arrow keys to explore the topics above and below the keyword you found. Then put the focus on the keywords “Graphics Labeler.”</li> <li>Press ENTER on “Graphics Labeler.” There is more than one Help topic associated with these keywords. Press the ARROW keys to explore the topics.</li> <li>Select Overview of the JAWS Utilities, and then press ENTER.</li> <li>Next, press F6 to move to the topic pane, and read the information about the topic.</li> <li>Press F6 to move back to the keyword entry box. Delete any word or phrase there, and then type cursors.</li> <li>Next, press TAB to move to that word in the list of keywords.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to select the next keyword, which is “JAWS cursor.”</li> <li>Continue to press DOWN ARROW to explore these. They are subkeywords of the term “cursors.” For example, JAWS cursor, PC cursor, and Virtual PC cursor. Subkeywords are used to provide more specific information about a broad or more general topic. For example, an index could have the term “Dogs” followed by the subkeywords “German Shepherd,” “Golden Retriever,” “Labrador,” and so on.</li> </ul> <h5 id="searching-the-help-system-1">Searching the Help System</h5> <p>You can use a full-text search to find information on keywords that don’t appear in the index or to find all topics where a certain word or phrase is used.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Next, you’ll learn how to use the JAWS Help system’s full text search feature.</p> <ul> <li><p>In JAWS, open the Help menu and choose Help Topics. Alternatively, just press F1 from within the JAWS window.</p></li> <li><p>Hold CTRL and press the TAB key until you move to the Search tab page. NOTE: If you are continuing from the exercise above you may need to press F6 to move back to the left side of the window first.</p></li> <li><p>Type the phrase, mouse pointer, and then press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the list of topics that contain the words you searched for. Make a note of how many topics are found. Use the UP and DOWN ARROW keys to explore this list. Notice that many topics were retrieved by the search. This is because the HTML Help system was looking for any topics that contained both of the two words contained in the first search. However, it was not looking to see if the words were next to each other in the text, or even if they were in the same sentence. It just found all topics containing both words at least once somewhere within each topic. NOTE: The search may also have found larger words that contain part of the text you search for. For example, the word “pointer” might be found as part of the plural “pointers.”</p></li> <li><p>Press ALT+W to move back to the keyword entry box. Type quotation marks around the phrase “mouse pointer,” and then press ENTER to retry the search.</p></li> <li><p>Press TAB to move to the search results list to view the results. Notice that about half as many topics were found this time. Select any of the topics found, and press ENTER.</p></li> <li><p>Then, press F6 to move to the topic pane so you can read the information.</p></li> <li><p>To find out exactly where the phrase appears in the topic, press CTRL+F. Type the phrase in the JAWS find dialog box and then press ENTER. Focus moves to a line of text that contains the current search phrase. You can verify this by reading the current line with INSERT+UP ARROW. Press F3 to move to each instance of the phrase and repeat the Say Line command to hear the new text that is found. For more information on the JAWS Find feature, read the prior Surf’s Up lesson on using the JAWS Find Command.</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="marking-favorite-topics-1">Marking Favorite Topics</h5> <p>You can bookmark topics you need to refer to regularly so you do not have to always look for them in the table of contents or through a search.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Use the JAWS help system to add or remove a favorite topic.</p> <ul> <li>In JAWS, open the Help menu and choose Help Topics. Alternatively, just press F1 from within the JAWS window.</li> <li>Hold CTRL and press the TAB key until you hear “Table of Contents page.”</li> <li>Select the book Using the Internet with JAWS and press RIGHT ARROW to open it.</li> <li>Select the book Navigating Web Pages and press RIGHT ARROW to open it.</li> <li>Select the topic Navigation Quick Keys and press ENTER to open this topic.</li> <li>Press CTRL+TAB until you hear “Favorites Page.” The title of the currently opened topic is displayed.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the Add button and press the SPACEBAR. Focus moves to the list of bookmarked topics which now includes the Navigation Quick Keys topic.</li> <li>Press ALT+F4 to close the JAWS help and then reopen it.</li> <li>Press CTRL+TAB until you reach the “Favorites Page” and press TAB to move to the list of bookmarked topics. The Navigation Quick Keys topic is still listed so you can press ENTER to open it and then F6 to move to the topic pane to read it. This saves you from having to navigate the table of contents to locate this topic each time you want to look up a navigation quick key.</li> <li>To remove a favorite topic from the list, press TAB to move to the Remove button and press SPACEBAR.</li> </ul> <h5 id="printing-html-help-topics-1">Printing HTML Help Topics</h5> <p>To print any topic in an HTML Help system, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Select the topic that you want to print in the table of contents, or find the topic using the index or search feature. Be sure to press F6 to move to the topic pane before continuing.</li> <li>Press CTRL+P to open the print dialog box.</li> <li>Select the printer you want to use, as well as any other options available. Then press ALT+P or ENTER to activate the Print button.</li> </ul> <h5 id="moving-back-to-the-previous-topic-1">Moving Back to the Previous Topic</h5> <p>While browsing through an HTML Help system, you can do the following to return to the previous topic:</p> <ul> <li>Press ALT+O to open the Options menu.</li> <li>Press B to choose Back. TIP: In JAWS Help, you can press ALT+B to move to the “Back” link at the bottom of each page. Press ENTER to activate this link and return to the previous page. You can also press ALT+X to move to the “Next” link at the bottom of each page. Additionally, you can also press ALT+LEFT ARROW to move to a prior HTML help page or ALT+RIGHT ARROW to move forward.</li> </ul> <h3 id="using-placemarkers-and-the-custom-placemarker-page-summary">Using PlaceMarkers and the Custom PlaceMarker Page Summary</h3> <h4 id="using-placemarkers-and-the-custom-placemarker-page-summary-1">Using PlaceMarkers and the Custom PlaceMarker Page Summary</h4> <h5 id="placemarkers">PlaceMarkers</h5> <p>PlaceMarkers allow you to quickly and easily navigate to commonly used areas of your favorite Web pages or HTML documents when using JAWS. You can use PlaceMarkers to jump between certain areas of a page, mark important sections of an HTML document, or indicate key form elements. For example, you could use PlaceMarkers to move to required fields in a complicated form or specific paragraphs in a long HTML document. Press the navigation quick key K to move to the next PlaceMarker, or press SHIFT+K to move to the prior PlaceMarker.</p> <p>A random selection of fictitious stock quotes for today are listed on the <a href="e-stocks.htm">E-Stocks sample page</a>.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Open the E-Stocks sample page, and follow along with the directions below to navigate to the table containing stock listings.</p> <ul> <li>Press CTRL+HOME to go to the top of the page.</li> <li>Press T to move to the table which contains stock listings.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW until you hear JAWS say “Change,” which is the third column. The first column has the stock symbol, and the second column has the stock price.</li> <li>Next, press CTRL+ALT+DOWN ARROW to move down to the second row and JAWS should say ATVI, which is the stock symbol in column one, followed by a number and a percentage. The number and the percentage are the amount of change for ATVI stock since the page was last updated.</li> </ul> <h6 id="inserting-placemarkers">Inserting PlaceMarkers</h6> <p>EXERCISE: Follow the steps below to put several PlaceMarkers in this table.</p> <ul> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+K to display the PlaceMarker list.</li> <li>Press ENTER to choose the Add button. An edit box appears with the number and the percentage taken from the Web page. This text is highlighted, so type over it and give this PlaceMarker the name of “ATVI.”</li> <li>Press ENTER to close the PlaceMarker dialog box.</li> <li>Press CTRL+ALT+DOWN ARROW two more times. You should hear JAWS identify that the focus is in the cell at the intersection of the row heading LEA and the column heading Change. You can press CTRL+ALT+NUM PAD 5 to read the current cell coordinates, column headings, and cell contents. Focus should be in column three, row four. This is the percentage change for the stock symbol LEA in column one.</li> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+K to display the PlaceMarker list.</li> <li>Press ENTER to create a new PlaceMarker. The text for the current price change and percentage should appear in the edit box that displays. Again, JAWS has taken text from the position of the virtual cursor on the page. Type in the stock symbol “LEA.”</li> <li>Press ENTER to close this dialog box.</li> <li>Press CTRL+ALT+DOWN ARROW two more times to move to the row containing the percentage change for the stock symbol NT in column one.</li> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+K to display the PlaceMarker list.</li> <li>Press ENTER to create a new PlaceMarker. Type “NT” to replace the suggested text taken from the Web page.</li> <li>Press ENTER to close this dialog box.</li> </ul> <h6 id="navigating-with-placemarkers">Navigating with PlaceMarkers</h6> <p>EXERCISE: Now, practice moving from one PlaceMarker to the next by pressing the navigation quick key K to move forward and SHIFT+K to move backwards.</p> <p>Notice that you will hear JAWS announce “wrapping to top” or “wrapping to bottom,” depending on the direction you are going when JAWS reaches either the bottom or the top of the page.</p> <p>EXERCISE: Next, take a few minutes to explore part of the PlaceMarker dialog box.</p> <ul> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+K to display the PlaceMarker list.</li> <li>Press INSERT+E to hear the default button in this dialog box. You should hear JAWS announce that the Add button is the default button.</li> <li>Press the SPACEBAR to select the first PlaceMarker in the list.</li> <li>Now press INSERT+E to read the default button. Notice that the default button is now Move To. This is a smart dialog box. Initially, when you first enter it, JAWS assumes that you want to add a new PlaceMarker. However, after you select an existing PlaceMarker in the list, JAWS assumes that you want to move to one of them.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to select the third PlaceMarker, “NT.”</li> <li>Press ENTER to move to this PlaceMarker. Notice that JAWS begins reading the text of the cell that the PlaceMarker is located in. JAWS remembers, down to the character, where you set your PlaceMarkers.</li> </ul> <h6 id="sharing-placemarkers">Sharing PlaceMarkers</h6> <p>PlaceMarkers remain in place even when you shut down JAWS and come back again. You can also share PlaceMarkers with other JAWS users. The PlaceMarkers are stored in the Settingsfolder. The file name will be the URL of the Web page followed by the file extension PMI.</p> <h6 id="other-placemarker-options">Other PlaceMarker Options</h6> <p>EXERCISE: Take a look at some of the other parts of the PlaceMarker dialog box.</p> <ul> <li>Press CTRL+SHIFT+K to display the PlaceMarker list.</li> <li>Press the SPACEBAR to select the first item in the list, which is the stock name ATVI in the second row.</li> <li>Press the TAB key to move to the Add button.</li> <li>Continue pressing the TAB key to explore the other buttons. You can change the name of a PlaceMarker, remove a PlaceMarker, or remove all PlaceMarkers.</li> <li>For now, press ESC to close the PlaceMarker list.</li> </ul> <h5 id="custom-placemarker-page-summary">Custom PlaceMarker Page Summary</h5> <p>EXERCISE: Use the custom PlaceMarker page summary to automatically read the stocks you want to monitor whenever you visit this page.</p> <p>To begin, do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Go to the <a href="e-stocks.htm">E-Stocks sample page</a> and press INSERT+V to display the JAWS Quick Settings dialog box. Focus is in the search edit box.</li> <li>Type “custom” without the quotes. The tree view below the search edit box changes to show settings containing the word custom.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Custom Page Summary in the General Options node of the tree view. By default, it shows Do Nothing.</li> <li>Use the SPACEBAR to choose either Speak PlaceMarkers On Page Load or List PlaceMarkers in Results Viewer On Page Load. If you choose Speak PlaceMarkers On Page Load, JAWS reads the custom PlaceMarker page summary from the PlaceMarker locations with speech only. If you choose List PlaceMarkers in Results Viewer On Page Load, JAWS displays the PlaceMarker page summary in the Results Viewer.</li> <li>Press TAB to move to the OK button, and then activate it with the SPACEBAR.</li> <li>Press F5 to refresh the E-Stocks sample page. You can also use the access key ALT+Q to activate the Update Quotes button on the page. NOTE: Firefox uses the SHIFT key in addition for access keys on Web pages. If you are using Firefox, press ALT+SHIFT+Q to activate the Update Quotes button.</li> </ul> <p>When the page refreshes, JAWS gives you a summary of the PlaceMarkers on this page with speech or with the Results Viewer, depending on how you set it. You hear each stock that you marked, and the change in that stock’s value. This is an example of how you can use the PlaceMarkers and the custom PlaceMarker page summary to track changes and updates to Web pages that you visit frequently.</p> <p>NOTE: To choose a custom PlaceMarker page summary that applies to all HTML pages for an entire domain, such as Vispero.com or Google.com, use the Personalized Settings feature of JAWS. When you press INSERT+V to start Quick Settings do the following:</p> <ul> <li>Type “custom” without the quotes. The tree view below the search edit box changes to show settings containing the word custom.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Custom Page Summary in the Personalized Web Settings node of the tree view. By default, it shows Do Nothing.</li> <li>Try changing the settings as described above. Personalized settings remain in effect the next time you go to any page on that domain. Personalized settings are discussed in a later module.</li> </ul> <p>To choose a custom PlaceMarker page summary setting that applies to all HTML pages, refer to <a href="example2.htm">Custom PlaceMarker Page Summary Step-by-Step Instructions</a>.</p> <h6 id="temporary-placemarkers">Temporary PlaceMarkers</h6> <p>You can create one temporary PlaceMarker per Web page by pressing CTRL+WINDOWS Key+K in the spot where you want to place it. The temporary PlaceMarker is also saved in the PMI file. You can only have one temporary PlaceMarker per page, but you can move it to a different location by pressing CTRL+WINDOWS Key+K again in a new spot on the page.</p> <h3 id="using-search-engines-to-find-information-on-the-web">Using Search Engines to Find Information on the Web</h3> <h4 id="using-search-engines-to-find-information-on-the-web-1">Using Search Engines to Find Information on the Web</h4> <h5 id="search-engines">Search Engines</h5> <p>Search engines on the World Wide Web are remotely accessible programs that let you do keyword searches for information on the Internet. There are several types of search engines and searches may cover titles of documents, URL’s, headers, or full text. Keep in mind that the results you get from one search engine may not match the results you get from another search engine. In fact, they are often different due to the way each search engine behaves. Therefore, it may actually be beneficial to use more than one search engine on a regular basis.</p> <p>In this section, we briefly look at Google and Bing. Web pages are often dynamic and can change at any time. As a result, you may find that if either site changes, your experience with JAWS may be different than what is described here.</p> <h5 id="google">Google</h5> <p>EXERCISE: Use the link below to go to the Google web site and follow along with the instructions.</p> <p>When you first go to the <a href="https://www.google.com">Google web site</a> there is a blinking cursor in the search edit box near the middle of the page. Forms mode comes on automatically when you go to a web page which has the focus set to a blinking cursor in an edit box. If for some reason forms mode does not come on automatically on your computer, you can also press ENTER to go into forms mode, or you can press INSERT+F5 to open the JAWS Select a Form Field dialog box.</p> <p>TIP: Mouse users can also click inside edit boxes and forms mode comes on automatically.</p> <p>If you use Chrome or Firefox as your browser, Google is the default search engine so you can also perform searches right from the address bar. To move to the address bar, just press ALT+D.</p> <p>Either way, as you begin typing, an autocomplete list may appear. You can press DOWN ARROW to move through the list and then ENTER to perform a search, or you can simply continue typing what you are searching for without using the list.</p> <p>After you have typed in some text, press ENTER to activate the Search button. Results appear on the page below. We will discuss some techniques for finding the results on the page in a moment. But first, Google only returns web pages that contain all of the words in your query. If you find that you get too many “hits” or web pages that match your search, you can enter more words in your search query to narrow the choices.</p> <p>Using good keywords gives you better results. Be as specific as you can. For example, a search for the keyword “musicians” will yield far more results than a search for the keywords “Elvis Presley.” You do not need to include “and” between terms, but the order in which you type your keywords will affect the search results. You can also search for a specific phrase by including words in quotation marks. Google searches are not case sensitive.</p> <p>You can also use the following items within your keywords for Google searches:</p> <ul> <li><ul> <li>(minus) sign. Causes Google to exclude a word from your search. For example, “JAWS” can refer to a screen reading software or a famous movie. You can exclude many of the movie-related hits by searching for “JAWS -movie.” (Be sure to include a space before the minus sign and no spaces between the minus sign and the word “movie.”) Searches for JAWS with different conditions yielded the following results: <ul> <li>JAWS, about 1,690,000,000 results</li> <li>JAWS windows -movie, still yields about the same number of results, but you find much more information about JAWS screen reader and very little, if any, information about movies. There will most likely still be links to videos on YouTube or other sources.</li> <li>“JAWS screen reader” (in quotes), about 49,600 results As you narrow your search and use better keywords, you get more relevant results. Putting a phrase into quotes tells Google to look for the exact words in that exact order.</li> </ul></li> </ul></li> </ul> <p>Try typing different things such as names, phone numbers, and more to find people or things.</p> <p>Try a search for Vispero. <a href="https://www.google.com">Use this link to go to the Google web site</a>. On the results page, there are a couple of things you can do to get more information about the results of the search:</p> <ul> <li>The statistics of your search are typically placed between the search edit box and the search results. You can use the JAWS find command CTRL+F to look for the word “Results,” and then read that line. For example, when testing this, the search found, “About 203,000,000 results (0.80 seconds).” This can be useful if you need to narrow the search.</li> <li>Google uses a “main” region to guide you to the search results. You can press R to move from one region to another.</li> <li>The items found as a result of your search are placed on the page as both links and headings. You can press the navigation quick key H to move quickly among the headings that match your search. Since they are also links, you can press ENTER to activate them and move to those web pages of interest.</li> <li>Below each heading (and link) that match your search is a short synopsis of what that page is about. After pressing H to move to a heading (link), just press DOWN ARROW to read the text below it for more information.</li> <li>Remember, you can also press SHIFT+H to move backwards.</li> <li>There is also a good structure to the headings. The search results are typically listed after a heading level two. The matches found for the search are typically level three headings. EXERCISE: Google uses regions to make navigation easier. Explore them by pressing R to move from region to region, and then press DOWN ARROW to move into the next section.</li> </ul> <p>You can also read through the search results page using normal reading keys or use INSERT+F7 to open the list of links and see what related links were found. Use the Move to Link button in the links list, ALT+M, to move to a particular link and then down arrow through the associated text to find out if this might be what you are looking for.</p> <p>In addition to the information displayed on the initial results page, there are often links to more pages of information that meet your search criteria. These pages are reached by activating the link for the number of the page. Usually you will find links for additional pages 2 through 10 near the bottom of each page, along with a Next link. Each page beyond the first page also contains a number of items that match your search.</p> <h6 id="google-search-tools">Google Search Tools</h6> <p>Google also provides easy-to-use search tools. For example:</p> <ul> <li>“Weather Chicago” yields the current weather in Chicago</li> <li>“25 kilometers in miles” converts kilometers to miles</li> <li>“Define screen magnification” yields definitions for screen magnification</li> <li>“Seafood restaurants 33716” yields restaurants that serve seafood in or near that zip code</li> <li>And so on… NOTE: For both the Google web site and the Bing web site discussed in the next section, be sure to check out the other links on their sites for Advanced Search, Help topics, and more.</li> </ul> <h5 id="bing">Bing</h5> <p>Bing is another popular search engine that many people use. As with Google, when you first go to the <a href="https://www.bing.com">Bing website</a> there is a blinking cursor in an edit box and JAWS should automatically turn on Forms mode. If you use Edge as your browser, Bing is also the default search engine so you can perform searches right from the address bar. To move to the address bar, just press ALT+D and begin typing what you want to search for.</p> <p>After you have typed in some text, press ENTER to activate the Search button.</p> <p>Bing behaves very much the same way as Google and displays a list of hits of matching items. These are links to further resources, and each link here also has a text description taken from that source that matches your query.</p> <p>After the Bing results page loads, press the letter H to move to the different headings on the page. Since the headings are also links, pressing ENTER on one takes you to the web page indicated. Beneath each heading/link is text that describes a little bit about that page. Press INSERT+F7 to use the list of links to explore the links, or you can also press TAB to move from one link to another.</p> <p>To find the number of matches, use the JAWS Find and look for the word “results” without the quotes. You may have to use the function key F3 to repeat the JAWS find. The results for Yahoo! are typically near the bottom of the page, so you may find the number of matches more quickly by pressing SHIFT+F3 to search backwards.</p> <p>Bing also has links to other results pages, just as Google does. These links show as numbers 2 through 5, along with a Next link, and are located near the bottom of the page.</p> <h5 id="changing-the-browsers-default-search-engine">Changing the Browser’s Default Search Engine</h5> <p>Typing your search query directly into your browser’s address bar is a fast and convenient way to locate information. For this to work, web browsers are configured to use a specific search engine. When searching from the address bar in Edge, results are displayed using Bing while searching from the address bar in Chrome or Firefox displays results using Google. If you prefer, you can change to a different search engine through your Browser’s settings. For instance, you may wish to have Edge use Google instead of Bing when searching from the address bar.</p> <p>Press ENTER on one of the following links to view information on changing the default search engine for your specific browser. After pressing ENTER, press DOWN ARROW to review the information.</p> <p><a href="javascript:unhide('ChangeEdge');">Change the Default Search Engine in Edge</a></p> <h6 id="change-the-default-search-engine-in-edge">Change the Default Search Engine in Edge</h6> <ul> <li>Press ALT+F to open the Settings and more menu and press S to open the Settings page. Focus is placed in the Search edit box.</li> <li>Press SHIFT+TAB to move to the menu of settings categories and press ENTER to activate Forms mode.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Privacy, search, and services and press ENTER to select this category.</li> <li>If Forms mode did not automatically turn off, press ESC to turn it off and then press H to move to the Services heading.</li> <li>Press B to move to the Address bar and search button and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press C to move to the list box that contains all of the search engines that can be used in the address bar. Press ENTER to turn on Forms mode, use the ARROW keys to select a different search engine, and press ENTER.</li> <li>Press CTRL+F4 to close the Settings page and your changes are automatically saved. <a href="javascript:unhide('ChangeChrome');">Change the Default Search Engine in Chrome</a></li> </ul> <h6 id="change-the-default-search-engine-in-chrome">Change the Default Search Engine in Chrome</h6> <ul> <li><p>Press ALT+F to open the Chrome menu and press S to open the Settings page. Focus is placed in the Search edit box.
