Hotkeys</a></li> </ul></li> </ul> <h4 id="vispero-account-frequently-asked-questions-1">Vispero Account – Frequently Asked Questions</h4> <h5 id="general-account-questions">General Account Questions</h5> <p>Do I need internet to use my Vispero software, or only to sign in?</p> <p>Internet access is required to create an account. Once you are signed in, you can use JAWS, ZoomText, or Fusion as you normally would, whether you are connected to the internet.</p> <p>How do I know if I already have a Vispero or Portal account?</p> <p>If you’ve signed in on our website, the Store, or the Vispero Portal using your email and a password, then you already have an account. If you’re unsure, try the “Forgot Password” option with your email address. If you currently manage your licenses through the Freedom Scientific Portal, nothing changes—you can continue using it as you always have.</p> <p>Can I use the same account for Home and Pro licenses?</p> <p>Yes. You can sign in with the same Vispero Account regardless of which license type you use. Your account is used for sign-in and does not change how your license works today.</p> <p>Can I change my login email address later?</p> <p>Yes, but this update must be done by Support. Call 1-800-444-4443 or use the Support form, and our team can help you update the email on your account.</p> <p>What if I have different work and home email addresses?</p> <p>You can choose the email that makes the most sense for you. Your choice of email for signing in does not affect how your license is handled.</p> <p>Does signing in affect privacy? Why do I need to choose a date-of-birth range? Is data collected?</p> <p>Signing in helps verify your identity and ensures the software behaves correctly for your age group. We do not collect personal usage data from JAWS, ZoomText, or Fusion as part of this process, and your license is not connected to your account today.</p> <p>Why is signing in required at all?</p> <p>Signing in helps confirm who is using the software and supports improvements to installation, updates, and future account-based features. It does not change how your license works today.</p> <h5 id="schools-and-students">Schools and Students</h5> <p>Do staff or students each need their own account?</p> <p>We recommend that each person has their own account, so it is linked to the correct individual. This also helps prepare users for future account-based features.</p> <p>How do minors or K–12 students create accounts? What birthdate should be used?</p> <p>They should use their real birthdate so the correct age-based behavior can be applied in our software.</p> <h5 id="shared-restricted-or-multi-device-environments">Shared, Restricted, or Multi-Device Environments</h5> <p>How do accounts work on shared or public computers?</p> <p>Users can sign in with their account and later sign out after using the computer.</p> <p>Can multiple installs or multiple devices use the same account?</p> <p>Yes, multiple devices can use the same account. We encourage users not to share their login information, so the account stays tied to the correct individual.</p> <h3 id="voice-assistant-in-the-classroom-1">Voice Assistant in the Classroom</h3> <ul> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/resources/">Resources</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/resources/blackboard-with-jaws-tutorials/">Blackboard with JAWS Tutorials</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/resources/use-jaws-with-canvas/">Use JAWS with the Canvas Learning Management System</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/resources/voice-assistant-in-the-classroom/">Voice Assistant in the Classroom</a></li> </ul> <h4 id="voice-assistant-in-the-classroom-2">Voice Assistant in the Classroom</h4> <p>For Teachers of the Visually Impaired (TVIs) working in early education, this page aims to introduce you to the benefits of utilizing JAWS Voice Assistant as a tool to expose your young students to synthesized speech and screen readers. The Voice Assistant serves as a helpful companion within JAWS, providing voice-activated access to selected JAWS features and helps empower your students and enhance their educational experience.</p> <h5 id="what-is-jaws-voice-assistant-sharky">What is JAWS Voice Assistant (Sharky)?</h5> <p>JAWS Voice Assistant, also known as Sharky, enables you to interact with various JAWS features using spoken commands. To issue a command, you must first say “Hey Sharkey.” This alerts Sharky that you are ready to speak a particular voice command. For example, “Hey Sharky, what time is it?”</p> <p>While Sharky provides voice-activated control over certain JAWS functions, it is important to note that it does not have complete control over the computer. This means that you will not be able to use Sharkey for things like saving or opening files, or accessing specific features in Windows.</p> <h5 id="benefits-of-jaws-voice-assistant-sharky-for-early-education">Benefits of JAWS Voice Assistant (Sharky) for Early Education</h5> <ul> <li>Accessible Learning: Sharky serves as a valuable tool to make computers and digital resources accessible to visually impaired students in the early stages of their education. It provides an engaging and interactive way for them to explore the digital world.</li> <li>Speech Synthesis Exposure: By utilizing Sharky, students are exposed to synthesized speech, which helps develop their auditory skills and learn to associate spoken words with on-screen content.</li> <li>Screen Reader Familiarity: Introducing Sharky at an early age helps students become familiar with screen reading technology. It establishes a foundation for future keyboarding skills and independent computer usage.</li> <li>Hands-Free Interaction: With Sharky, students can use voice commands to navigate the computer, interact with applications, read documents, and perform selected tasks. This hands-free interaction encourages independence and boosts confidence.</li> </ul> <h5 id="getting-started-with-jaws-voice-assistant-sharky">Getting Started with JAWS Voice Assistant (Sharky)</h5> <p>To introduce Sharky to your early education students, follow these steps:</p> <ul> <li><p>Ensure JAWS is installed on the computer your students will be using. Contact your school’s IT department for assistance if needed.</p></li> <li><p>Voice Assistant (Sharky) should be enabled by default when you start JAWS. To confirm this, press INSERT+J to open the JAWS application window, open the Utilities menu, select the Voice Assistant submenu, and choose Settings. While in the Voice Assistant Settings dialog, you can also make sure Sharky is using the correct microphone.</p></li> <li><p>Familiarize yourself with the wake word, “Hey Sharky,” which is used to begin any voice command.</p></li> <li><p>Consider showing a video demonstration or perform a live demo of Sharky in action, highlighting how to activate Sharky with the wake word and performing selected tasks within JAWS.</p></li> <li><p>Guide students through the process of activating Sharky by saying “Hey Sharky” and using voice commands to perform selected JAWS functions. Encourage active listening and appropriate interactions.</p></li> <li><p>Allow students to independently interact with Sharky and use voice commands for selected JAWS functions. Provide support as needed to ensure a positive experience. Here are a few voice commands that may be useful for practicing with your students.</p></li> <li><p>Check the time: “Hey Sharky, what time is it?”</p></li> <li><p>Check the current date: “Hey Sharky, what is today’s date?”</p></li> <li><p>Check the computer’s battery and network connection status: “Hey Sharky, battery.”</p></li> <li><p>Turn JAWS Keyboard Help on or off: “Hey Sharky, toggle Keyboard Help.”</p></li> <li><p>Have JAWS tell a joke: “Hey Sharky, tell me a joke.”</p></li> <li><p>Increase voice rate: “Hey Sharky, speak faster.”</p></li> <li><p>Decrease voice rate: “Hey Sharky, speak slower.”</p></li> <li><p>Select text: “Hey Sharky, start selection.” Use the ARROW keys to move to the end of the text you want to select and then, “Hey Sharky, finish selection,” to select all content between the two locations.</p></li> <li><p>Access JAWS settings: “Hey Sharky, Settings.”</p></li> <li><p>Close and restart JAWS: “Hey Sharky, restart JAWS.”</p></li> </ul> <h5 id="complete-listings-of-all-supported-voice-commands">Complete Listings of All Supported Voice Commands</h5> <p>The following are examples of supported and suggested voice commands to perform various actions. Practice and try your own variations of these commands. href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/category/webinar/zoom/">Zoom</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/category/webinar/zoomtext/">ZoomText</a></li> </ul> <h3 id="zoomtext-faq">ZoomText FAQ</h3> <h4 id="zoomtext-faq-1">ZoomText FAQ</h4> <h5 id="what-is-zoomtext-1">What is ZoomText?</h5> <p>ZoomText® is screen magnification software for the Microsoft Windows operating system. It allows you to change screen colors and magnification levels, customize the mouse pointer and text cursor to make it easy to find them, and turn on a focus rectangle to help you track where you are on the screen. Additionally, ZoomText is available with some basic speech features for reading documents, web pages, and email, as well as hearing what you are typing or what is under the mouse pointer.</p> <h5 id="who-is-zoomtext-for-1">Who is ZoomText for?</h5> <p>ZoomText is for any user with enough vision to see a computer screen, but requires extra visual enhancements to be able to more comfortably read screen content.</p> <h5 id="what-operating-systems-does-zoomtext-work-with-1">What operating systems does ZoomText work with?</h5> <p>ZoomText installs and works with Windows® 11, Windows 10, Windows Server® 2022, Windows Server 2019, and Windows Server 2016. Note that as Windows continues to change, new ZoomText features may not be available in older versions of Windows.</p> <h5 id="what-versions-of-microsoft-office-does-zoomtext-support-1">What versions of Microsoft Office does ZoomText support?</h5> <p>ZoomText works with Microsoft Office 365, or Microsoft Office 2016 and later. ZoomText also supports older versions of Office (2013 and 2010), however, there are no further enhancements coming for these older versions.</p> <p>ZoomText has been tested to perform best with the latest Windows operating systems and software applications. As new versions of Freedom Scientific products are released, support for older software may not continue.</p> <h5 id="what-web-browsers-does-zoomtext-work-with-1">What web browsers does ZoomText work with?</h5> <p>ZoomText visually tracks as you navigate websites in Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and Internet Explorer. Support for Microsoft Edge is continuing to improve as well. Web pages are also read aloud if you have ZoomText Magnifier/Reader.</p> <h5 id="does-zoomtext-read-pdf-documents-1">Does ZoomText read PDF documents?</h5> <p>Yes. ZoomText’s visual features work to help you navigate in PDF documents. If you have ZoomText Magnifier/Reader, the document will also be read aloud.</p> <h5 id="can-i-read-my-email-with-zoomtext-1">Can I read my email with ZoomText?</h5> <p>Yes. Special attention has gone into the design of ZoomText to make sure you have full access to email, especially with Microsoft Outlook from Office 365.</p> <h5 id="what-is-the-difference-between-zoomtext-magnifier-and-zoomtext-magnifierreader-1">What is the difference between ZoomText Magnifier and ZoomText Magnifier/Reader?</h5> <p>ZoomText Magnifier contains all of the visual enhancements necessary to help make content on your computer screen easier to see. These include selection of the zoom level, zoom window types, screen enhancements, and navigation options. No speech feedback is available.</p> <p>ZoomText Magnifier/Reader offers all of the features of ZoomText Magnifier with the addition of speech features including typing, mouse and program echo; the AppReader and Reading Zones tools, and the Text Cursor and commands for speaking certain items like the window title and the time or date.</p> <h5 id="is-zoomtext-magnifierreader-intended-to-be-a-complete-magnification-and-screen-reading-solution-1">Is ZoomText Magnifier/Reader intended to be a complete magnification and screen reading solution?</h5> <p>No. ZoomText Magnifier/Reader is still primarily for low vision users with some added speech functionality to help with certain tasks like reading documents and web pages, echoing your typing or mouse movement, and speaking other essential program activity. If your vision has deteriorated enough where you need more speech feedback than what is provided by ZoomText Magnifier/Reader, then you should <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/Products/LowVision/Fusion">check out Fusion</a> which combines both ZoomText and JAWS for the best in screen magnification and screen reading functionality.</p> <h5 id="where-can-i-buy-zoomtext-1">Where can I buy ZoomText?</h5> <p>ZoomText is available from Freedom Scientific or your local Freedom Scientific dealer. Visit the <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/Forms/DealerLocator">Dealer Locator page</a> to find out who serves your area.</p> <h5 id="if-i-already-own-zoomtext-can-i-upgrade-to-zoomtext-magnifierreader-or-to-fusion-1">If I already own ZoomText, can I upgrade to ZoomText Magnifier/Reader or to Fusion?</h5> <p>Absolutely! Contact Freedom Scientific or your <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/Forms/DealerLocator">local dealer</a> for details and to place your order.</p> <h5 id="is-zoomtext-available-in-languages-other-than-english-1">Is ZoomText available in languages other than English?</h5> <p>ZoomText is available in many languages, some of which can be obtained from the <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/Downloads/ZoomText">Freedom Scientific downloads pages</a>. Additional languages are also available directly from your local distributor in many countries.</p> <h5 id="is-a-zoomtext-demo-available-1">Is a ZoomText demo available?</h5> <p>Yes, like other Freedom Scientific products, ZoomText can be installed and will work in a 40-minute mode. When that expires, reboot and it will work again in the same way. And, if an update comes out, it will alert you and allow it to update just as it does for licensed software.</p> <p>ZoomText is screen magnification software for the Microsoft Windows operating system. id="access-pdfs-in-adobe-acrobat-reader-with-jaws-2">Access PDFs in Adobe Acrobat Reader with JAWS</h3> <h4 id="access-pdfs-in-adobe-acrobat-reader-with-jaws-3">Access PDFs in Adobe Acrobat Reader with JAWS</h4> <p>August 15, 2024</p> <h5 id="description-and-objectives">Description and Objectives:</h5> <p>Portable Document Format (PDF) files are commonly used to share documents across platforms. These documents are widely used and often required in school and employment settings. They can include text and visuals such as images, charts, and tables to convey information.</p> <p>In this presentation we provide an overview of the Acrobat Reader interface, discuss accessible versus inaccessible PDFs, and provide tips on how to create accessible PDFs. We’ll show you how to:</p> <ul> <li>Install and set up Acrobat Reader</li> <li>Set preferences and accessibility settings</li> <li>Open PDFs in a web browser or Acrobat Reader</li> <li>Navigate and save a PDF</li> <li>Use JAWS Convenient OCR to read inaccessible PDFs</li> </ul> <h5 id="freedom-scientific-presenters">Freedom Scientific Presenters:</h5> <p>Elizabeth Whitaker and Rachel Buchanan</p> <h5 id="help-us-spread-the-word-6">Help Us Spread the Word:</h5> <p>Please feel free to share this with someone you think might benefit from attending.</p> <p><a href="https://doccenter.freedomscientific.com/doccenter/archives/2024_08_15_Acrobat_Reader/Access-PDFs-in-Adobe-Acrobat-Reader-with-JAWS.mp3">Access PDFs in Adobe Acrobat Reader with JAWS (MP3)</a></p> <p>Note: If you want to save the MP3 and listen to it later, select the link to start the MP3 and then press CTRL+S.</p> <p><a href="https://doccenter.freedomscientific.com/doccenter/archives/2024_08_15_Acrobat_Reader/Access-PDFs-in-Adobe-Acrobat-Reader-with-JAWS.mp4">Access PDFs in Adobe Acrobat Reader with JAWS (MP4)</a></p> <p><a href="https://doccenter.freedomscientific.com/doccenter/archives/2024_08_15_Acrobat_Reader/Create-Accessible-Documents.pdf">Resource file for Creating Accessible Documents (PDF)</a></p> <p>Go To Complete List Of Archived Webinars</p> <h3 id="ai-tips-tools-and-techniques-where-to-begin-2">AI Tips, Tools, and Techniques: Where to Begin</h3> <h4 id="ai-tips-tools-and-techniques-where-to-begin-3">AI Tips, Tools, and Techniques: Where to Begin</h4> <p>September 4, 2025</p> <h5 id="objectives-1">Objectives:</h5> <p>Are you ready to start using artificial intelligence with JAWS, ZoomText, or Fusion but not sure where to begin? If so, join Liz, Ron, Rachel and Jose as they explain what to do, “When JAWS Does the Unexpected: Top five JAWS Troubleshooting Tips.”</p> <h5 id="freedom-scientific-presenters-38">Freedom Scientific Presenters:</h5> <p>Elizabeth Whitaker, Rachel Buchanan, Jose Tamayo, and Ron Miller</p> <h5 id="objectives-53">Objectives:</h5> <p>We’ll discuss important JAWS settings and keyboard commands for acquiring details about your environment, plus show you how to:</p> <ul> <li>Virtualize a control or window to gather information or copy error messages.</li> <li>Restore JAWS Factory settings to clear manually configured settings or custom-imported settings from a previous release of JAWS.</li> <li>Manually shutdown JAWS when an issue occurs.</li> <li>Restart JAWS using a layered command.</li> <li>Use JAWS Speech History to review and copy information spoken by JAWS. <a href="https://doccenter.freedomscientific.com/doccenter/archives/2023_02_16_Troubleshooting_Tips/When-JAWS-Does-the-Unexpected-Top-Five-Troubleshooting-Tips.mp3">When JAWS Does the Unexpected: Top Five JAWS Troubleshooting Tips (MP3)</a></li> </ul> <p>Note: If you would like to save the MP3 and listen to it later, select the link to start the MP3 and then press CTRL+S.</p> <p><a href="https://doccenter.freedomscientific.com/doccenter/archives/2023_02_16_Troubleshooting_Tips/When-JAWS-Does-the-Unexpected-Top-Five-Troubleshooting-Tips.mp4">When JAWS Does the Unexpected: Top Five JAWS Troubleshooting Tips (MP4)</a></p> <p>Go To Complete List Of Archived Webinars</p> <h3 id="word-tips-and-tricks-from-power-users-2">Word, Tips and Tricks from Power Users</h3> <h4 id="word-tips-and-tricks-from-power-users-3">Word, Tips and Tricks from Power Users</h4> <p>June 17, 2021</p> <p>Included in the Microsoft Office suite, Word is used to write and edit documents. Complete List Of Archived Webinars</p> <h2 id="miscellaneous-1">Miscellaneous</h2> <h3 id="passing-keystrokes-and-typing-text-with-scripts">10.0 Passing Keystrokes and Typing Text with Scripts</h3> <h4 id="passing-keystrokes-and-typing-text-with-scripts-1">10.0 Passing Keystrokes and Typing Text with Scripts</h4> <p>People new to writing scripts with JAWS often find it hard to differentiate between JAWS and Windows keystrokes. For example, the script writers at Freedom Scientific have attached scripts to common Windows keystrokes such as CTRL+C and CTRL+V, copy and paste. When you press either keystroke, Windows still copies and pastes using these keystrokes. However, something else also happens; when you press CTRL+C JAWS speaks “copied selection to clipboard.” Likewise, when you press CTRL+V, JAWS says, “Pasted from clipboard.” These messages let you know the expected action has taken place.</p> <p>The scripts associated with these keystrokes are examples of “pass-through” scripts. It is called a pass-through script because JAWS intercepts the keystroke before it reaches the application and performs the associated script. The script adds some type of extra functionality to the keystroke and then passes the keystroke through to the application. In this case the added functionality is the message JAWS speaks to notify you the action has been completed.</p> <p>In this chapter, you will learn how to capture keystrokes, add extra functionality to those keystrokes and pass them through to the active application. You will learn how to access menu bars and give keyboard access to commands in the menu system. You will also learn how to type text using scripts.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-4">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 10.0 Passing Keystrokes and Typing Text with Scripts, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="10-1_PassThroughScripts.htm">10.1 Pass-Through Scripts</a></p> <p><a href="10-2_GivingKeyboardAccess.htm">10.2 Giving Keyboard Access</a></p> <p><a href="10-3_DelayingYourScript.htm">10.3 Delaying Your Script</a></p> <p><a href="10-4_TypingText.htm">10.4 Typing Text</a></p> <p><a href="10-5_ChapterExercises.htm">10.5 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="10-1_PassThroughScripts.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="using-the-virtual-viewer">11.0 Using the Virtual Viewer</h3> <h4 id="using-the-virtual-viewer-1">11.0 Using the Virtual Viewer</h4> <p>When you press INSERT+H or INSERT+W to display hot key help, JAWS displays the keystrokes within the virtual viewer. Likewise, when you press INSERT+F1 to review screen sensitive help, JAWS displays the information in the virtual viewer as well.</p> <p>When JAWS displays information in the virtual viewer, the virtual cursor is active. You can use normal navigation keystrokes to read, select, and copy selected text to the clipboard.</p> <p>The virtual viewer is a Virtual Buffer you create using the Scripting Language and is a part of JAWS. The virtual viewer is also known as the user buffer. Text displayed in the virtual viewer is black on a white background, has a font size of 12 and a font type of Arial. The text displayed in the virtual viewer is identical to text found in any word processor or text editor.</p> <p>In this chapter, you will learn how to display messages in the virtual viewer. You will also learn how to create keystroke links within the virtual viewer.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-5">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 11.0 Using the Virtual Viewer, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="11-1_CheckingTheVirtualViewerStatus.htm">11.1 Checking the Virtual Viewer Status</a></p> <p><a href="11-2_CreatingTheMessages.htm">11.2 Creating the Messages</a></p> <p><a href="11-3_DisplayingTheMessages.htm">11.3 Displaying the Messages</a></p> <p><a href="11-4_DisplayingKeystrokesAsLinks.htm">11.4 Displaying Keystrokes as Links</a></p> <p><a href="11-5_ChapterExercises.htm">11.5 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="11-1_CheckingTheVirtualViewerStatus.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="understanding-functions">12.0 Understanding Functions</h3> <h4 id="understanding-functions-1">12.0 Understanding Functions</h4> <p>In previous chapters, you created scripts that performed a variety of actions ranging from speaking messages to typing keystrokes and more. Each time you wanted to perform the script, you pressed the assigned keystroke and JAWS performed the associated script.</p> <p>As you created these scripts, you called upon “built-in” functions. These types of functions are actually part of JAWS. Unlike the scripts you previously created, you will not find built-in functions within a JAWS script source file.</p> <p>While built-in functions are not contained within the JAWS script source file, “user-defined functions” are.</p> <p>User-defined functions are written both by Freedom Scientific and JAWS script developers. You create user-defined functions using the Script Manager.</p> <p>In addition to built-in and user-defined functions, there are also “event” functions. JAWS automatically performs event functions each time an associated event occurs in the Windows operating system. For example, each time you press TAB to move from control to control within a dialog, you are causing the “focus changed” event to occur. Although you can see these functions within the script files that come with JAWS, you cannot create your own event functions.</p> <p>This chapter introduces you to built-in and user-defined functions. You will gain a better understanding of built-in functions and their use. You will also learn how to create a user-defined function, pass parameters to a function, and return values using functions.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-6">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 12.0 Understanding Functions, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="12-1_OverviewOfFunctions.htm">12.1 Functions, An Overview</a></p> <p><a href="12-2_Built-inFunctions.htm">12.2 Built-in Functions</a></p> <p><a href="12-3_UserDefinedFunctions.htm">12.3 User-defined Functions</a></p> <p><a href="12-4_FunctionsThatReturnValues.htm">12.4 Functions that Return Values</a></p> <p><a href="12-5_TheUseStatement.htm">12.5 The Use Statement</a></p> <p><a href="12-6_ChapterExercises.htm">12.6 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="12-1_OverviewOfFunctions.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="windows-program-structure">13.0 Windows Program Structure</h3> <h4 id="windows-program-structure-1">13.0 Windows Program Structure</h4> <p>Most people who use the Windows operating system never really understand what the word “window” actually means. Most users realize the rectangular box that appears on the screen when a new application is opened is a window. They probably think of the text area of their word processor as a window as well.</p> <p>In most applications, every dialog box, menu, button, edit field, list box, etc. is actually a separate window with one or more identifiers that can be used to refer to it. However, a programmer may choose to create controls, such as entry fields, without making them actual windows. Programs like this are the most difficult to make accessible because there’s no simple way to identify and speak the various controls.</p> <p>In this chapter you will learn about Windows program structure and hierarchy. You will learn about different types of windows and how they are identified by the operating system. You will learn how to determine characteristics that uniquely identify windows. You will also learn how to use JAWS to explore the window structure of an application.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-7">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 13.0 Windows Program Structure, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="13-1_WindowsHierarchy.htm">13.1 Windows Hierarchy</a></p> <p><a href="13-2_ReassigningWindowClasses.htm">13.2 Reassigning Window Classes</a></p> <p><a href="13-3_ScriptUtilityMode.htm">13.3 The Script Utility Mode</a></p> <p><a href="13-4_CustomizingUnknownApplications.htm">13.4 Customizing an Unknown Application</a></p> <p><a href="13-5_DebuggingScripts.htm">13.5 Debugging Script Files</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="13-1_WindowsHierarchy.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="the-keyboard-manager">2.0 The Keyboard Manager</h3> <h4 id="the-keyboard-manager-1">2.0 The Keyboard Manager</h4> <p>You control the assignment of keystrokes to JAWS commands using the Keyboard Manager. The Keyboard Manager stores keystroke assignments in key map files, which have the extension of .jkm. You usually assign keystrokes to scripts at the time the script is created using the Script Manager. You can use the Keyboard Manager to view, add, change, or delete keystroke assignments.</p> <p>The Keyboard Manager has a screen layout that consists of a left hand pane and a right hand pane. Press TAB and SHIFT+TAB to move between the two panes. Press UP and DOWN ARROW to move up and down either side of the manager.</p> <p>For a list of all keyboard commands available in the Keyboard Manager, see <a href="Appendix_B.htm">Appendix B: Keyboard Manager Commands</a>.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-8">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 2.0 The Keyboard Manager, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="02-1_StartingTheKeyboardManager.htm">2.1 Starting the Keyboard Manager</a></p> <p><a href="02-2_KeyboardManagerFiles.htm">2.2 Keyboard Manager Files</a></p> <p><a href="02-3_KeyboardManagerLeftHandPane.htm">2.3 Keyboard Manager, Left Hand Pane</a></p> <p><a href="02-4_KeyboardManagerRightHandPane.htm">2.4 Keyboard Manager, Right Hand Pane</a></p> <p><a href="02-5_FindingKeystrokes.htm">2.5 Finding Keystrokes</a></p> <p><a href="02-6_ReviewingScriptDocumentation.htm">2.6 Reviewing Scripting Documentation</a></p> <p><a href="02-7_AddingChangingAndRemovingKeystrokes.htm">2.7 Adding, Changing, and Removing Keystrokes</a></p> <p><a href="02-8_KeyboardManagerOptions.htm">2.8 Keyboard Manager Options</a></p> <p><a href="02-9_ChapterExercises.htm">2.9 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="02-1_StartingTheKeyboardManager.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="what-are-scripts">3.0 What are Scripts?</h3> <h4 id="what-are-scripts-1">3.0 What are Scripts?</h4> <p>You can think of a script as a mini computer program that contains sequences of individual steps used to activate and control a wide variety of computer processes. The action a script performs ranges from tasks as simple as entering repetitive strings of data to many of the standard routines your computer does on an ongoing basis as part of its operation.</p> <p>Scripts or combinations of scripts and functions control most JAWS behavior. Scripts analyze what actions are taking place in an application and determine how to handle the screen reading for you.</p> <p>Script files also contain functions. Like a script, a function is also a sequence of statements that perform a given task. However, functions differ from scripts in that you cannot activate them with a keystroke.</p> <p>You create scripts and functions with the Script Manager. You use a standard set of programming codes, formats, and rules to create your scripts and functions. After you have written your script or function, you compile your script or function into machine-readable language, so that the computer can understand the instructions. Once you compile your script or function, they are ready for your use.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-9">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 3.0 What are Scripts?, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="03-1_JAWSScriptsAndScriptFiles.htm">3.1 JAWS Scripts and Script Files</a></p> <p><a href="03-2_ProcessingKeystrokes.htm">3.2 Processing Keystrokes</a></p> <p><a href="03-3_PerformingFunctions.htm">3.3 Performing Functions</a></p> <p><a href="03-4_ScriptsVsFunctions.htm">3.4 Scripts vs. Functions</a></p> <p><a href="03-5_ChapterExercises.htm">3.5 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="03-1_JAWSScriptsAndScriptFiles.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="the-script-manager">4.0 The Script Manager</h3> <h4 id="the-script-manager-1">4.0 The Script Manager</h4> <p>The Script Manager provides you with all the tools you need to write, modify, and use scripts.</p> <p>The Script Manager is a full-featured text editor. In addition to the usual features contained in most text editors, it has built in capabilities to help you create scripts. You can insert functions into your new scripts, display reference information about functions and scripts that have already been written, check for errors that violate the rules of correct script writing, and save and compile your script files. In addition to providing full scripting capabilities for JAWS, the Script Manager can also be used to create scripts for the MAGic Pro Scripting Edition.</p> <p>The Script Manager provides hot keys you can use to read through the scripts in your script file more efficiently. For example, a script file can contain one or more scripts. You can use the function key F2 to move forward from script to script, or SHIFT+F2 to move backward from script to script. You can use the hot key combination, CTRL+L, to display a list of all scripts in the current file in alphabetic order.</p> <p>When you save your script file in the Script Manager with the keystroke, CTRL+S, the Script Manager automatically performs an additional step not found in other text editors and compiles your script file. Compiling a script converts the file from text to machine-readable information.</p> <p>The Script Manager saves the original text file with a .jss (JAWS Script Source) file extension, and the compiled or binary version (machine-readable language) is saved with a .jsb (JAWS Script Binary) file extension. This is why it is always important to create and save your script files using the Script Manager. If you edit and save your files using some other text editor such as Notepad, they are not compiled when you save them, and JAWS will be unaware of the changes you have made.</p> <p>For a list of all keyboard commands available in the Script Manager, see <a href="Appendix_C.htm">Appendix C: Script Manager Commands</a>.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-10">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 4.0 The Script Manager, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="04-1_ScriptManagerFiles.htm">4.1 Script Manager Files</a></p> <p><a href="04-2_StartingTheScriptManager.htm">4.2 Starting the Script Manager</a></p> <p><a href="04-3_NavigatingScriptFiles.htm">4.3 Navigating Script Files</a></p> <p><a href="04-4_FindingAndReplacingText.htm">4.4 Finding and Replacing Text</a></p> <p><a href="04-5_ViewingInformation.htm">4.5 Viewing Information</a></p> <p><a href="04-6_ChapterExercises.htm">4.6 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="04-1_ScriptManagerFiles.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="reading-information-with-scripts">6.0 Reading Information with Scripts</h3> <h4 id="reading-information-with-scripts-1">6.0 Reading Information with Scripts</h4> <p>You learned about the Script Manager and used it to create your first two scripts in <a href="04-0_TheScriptManager.htm">Chapter 4</a> and <a href="05-0_CreatingScripts.htm">Chapter 5</a>. You created scripts that simply spoke messages when you pressed the appropriate keystroke.</p> <p>In this chapter, you will learn how to use the scripting language to read areas of the screen by moving various cursors. As you create scripts that read parts of a window, you should understand the differences between the various cursors and how they can be manipulated through a script or function.</p> <p>JAWS has three cursors you can use to read areas of the screen:</p> <ul> <li>PC cursor</li> <li>JAWS cursor</li> <li>Invisible cursor Manipulating cursors to read information is not the most efficient method of accessing that information. However, as a beginning scripter, you can use cursor manipulation as a quick way to write scripts to read information within a given window. You do not need to know the relationship between windows or the types of windows your scripts are accessing. As your knowledge of the scripting language grows, you will learn how to create scripts that read information more efficiently using advanced techniques.</li> </ul> <h5 id="table-of-contents-11">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 6.0 Reading Information with Scripts, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="06-1_BeforeYouWriteTheScript.htm">6.1 Before You Write the Script</a></p> <p><a href="06-2_PCCursor.htm">6.2 PC Cursor</a></p> <p><a href="06-3_JAWSCursor.htm">6.3 JAWS Cursor</a></p> <p><a href="06-4_InvisibleCursor.htm">6.4 Invisible Cursor</a></p> <p><a href="06-5_BeforeYouMoveACursor.htm">6.5 Before You Move a Cursor</a></p> <p><a href="06-6_MovingTheCursor.htm">6.6 Moving the Cursor</a></p> <p><a href="06-7_SpeakingTheInformation.htm">6.7 Speaking the Information</a></p> <p><a href="06-8_ChapterExercises.htm">6.8 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="06-1_BeforeYouWriteTheScript.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="creating-and-speaking-messages">8.0 Creating and Speaking Messages</h3> <h4 id="creating-and-speaking-messages-1">8.0 Creating and Speaking Messages</h4> <p>In this chapter, you will learn how to create messages using the JAWS message format. You will learn how to create your messages within a JAWS script message, (.jsm) file. You will also learn how to use long and short messages to honor your verbosity settings.</p> <p>In the previous chapters, you created scripts using built-in speaking functions that used hard-coded messages. A hard-coded message is a string of text typed directly in a function as a parameter.</p> <p>Each time you need to change the contents of the message, you must search the entire file for the message. Once you have located the message, you have to modify the message being careful not to forget the quotation marks surrounding the message. You have to do this with each message contained in your script file.</p> <p>Rather than using hard-coded messages, you can store all of your messages in a JAWS script message file (.jsm). This makes it easier to find all of your messages as they are all in one place. If you ever need to modify one or more of the messages, you need only to go to the message file and make the change once. You can include your message in any number of script files using the include statement.</p> <p>When you make changes to any of the messages in your message file, you must recompile each script file that includes the message file. You must take this extra step so that JAWS sees the changes to your messages.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-12">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 8.0 Creating and Speaking Messages, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="08-1_JAWSMessageConstants.htm">8.1 JAWS Message Constants</a></p> <p><a href="08-2_TheJAWSMessageFormat.htm">8.2 The JAWS Message Format</a></p> <p><a href="08-3_FormattingYourMessages.htm">8.3 Formatting Your Messages</a></p> <p><a href="08-4_SpeakingYourMessages.htm">8.4 Speaking Your Messages</a></p> <p><a href="08-5_ChapterExercises.htm">8.5 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="08-1_JAWSMessageConstants.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="controlling-the-flow-of-scripts-with-decision-making">9.0 Controlling the Flow of Scripts with Decision Making</h3> <h4 id="controlling-the-flow-of-scripts-with-decision-making-1">9.0 Controlling the Flow of Scripts with Decision Making</h4> <p>In the previous chapters, you created scripts that performed each line once and only once. When JAWS performs your scripts in this manner, each statement is performed regardless of any situations that may arise during the execution of the script. This manner of performing your scripts is called sequential flow control.</p> <p>This is the most basic way in which JAWS performs your scripts. JAWS performs each statement sequentially beginning with the first statement in your script and continuing to the EndScript statement. You can think of a script that flows sequentially as a script that JAWS performs step-by-step.</p> <p>In addition to creating scripts that JAWS performs sequentially, you can add statements to your scripts that perform an evaluation. This type of flow control is called branching, conditional, or decision-making.</p> <p>You may find that at some point during the execution of your script, the script must evaluate certain conditions before continuing. The conditions your script evaluates can be anything from the value contained within a variable to the return value from a function. Once your script completes the evaluation, the statements that are processed next are based on the outcome of the evaluation. When the outcome of the evaluation is true, processing may continue down one branch. If the outcome is found to be false, a second branch of statements is performed.</p> <p>For example, suppose you come to a group of two doors at the end of a hallway. Before you continue, you must evaluate which door to go through. Your decision will be based on a set of conditions. If it is dark outside, you might choose one door but if it is light out, you might choose another.</p> <p>Your script may need to do that same type of decision making. You use the If-Then-Else statement structure to make a decision. When your script comes to the If-Then-Else statement a condition is evaluated. Based on the outcome of the evaluation, your script may perform one branch of code as opposed to another.</p> <p>In this chapter, you will learn how to create basic If statements to make decisions in your scripts. You will learn the structure of the If statement and the uses of the Else and ElIf key words. You will also learn how to create more complex If statements that use compound evaluations as well as nesting If statements inside one another. You will also learn how to create a loop that executes a section of code multiple times.</p> <h5 id="table-of-contents-13">Table of Contents</h5> <p>Chapter 9.0 Controlling the Flow of Scripts with Decision Making, contains the following sections:</p> <p><a href="09-1_LogicalOperators.htm">9.1 Logical Operators</a></p> <p><a href="09-2_TheIfStatement.htm">9.2 The If Statement</a></p> <p><a href="09-3_TheElseStatement.htm">9.3 Adding a Second Branch, the Else Keyword</a></p> <p><a href="09-4_TheElIfStatement.htm">9.4 Adding Multiple Branches, the ElIf Statement</a></p> <p><a href="09-5_NestedIfStatements.htm">9.5 Nested If Statements</a></p> <p><a href="09-6_CompoundIfStatements.htm">9.6 Compound If Statements</a></p> <p><a href="09-7_Looping.htm">9.7 Looping</a></p> <p><a href="09-8_ChapterExercises.htm">9.8 Chapter Exercises</a></p> <p><a href="javascript:window.history.go(-1);">Back</a></p> <p><a href="09-1_LogicalOperators.htm">Next</a></p> <h3 id="accessibility-policy">Accessibility Policy</h3> <h4 id="accessibility-policy-1">Accessibility Policy</h4> <p>As the largest worldwide manufacturer of assistive technology products for those who are blind or have low vision, Freedom Scientific is committed to providing a website with the highest accessibility standards for all people with disabilities, including visual impairments, learning disabilities, physical impairments, and other forms of disability.</p> <h5 id="accessibility-standards">Accessibility Standards</h5> <p>Our website uses the <a href="https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/">WCAG 2.1</a> guidelines from the <a href="http://www.w3.org/WAI/PF/">World Wide Web Consortium (W3C)</a>. It also uses criteria included in the Section 508 Refresh Report, the proposed new <a href="https://www.access-board.gov/guidelines-and-standards/communications-and-it/about-the-ict-refresh">Section 508 Standards</a>.</p> <p>Content-bearing images may use alternative attributes (alt-text) to identify the image. All pages contain a “Skip to Main Content” link to facilitate navigation by screen readers and other non-mouse modes of input. Many of these design elements help people with eye conditions such as macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa.</p> <p>If you have any recommendations to further improve the experience on the Freedom Scientific website, please contact us.</p> <h3 id="accessing-math-content-with-jaws-and-fusion-miscellaneous">Accessing Math Content with JAWS and Fusion (Miscellaneous)</h3> <ul> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/teachers/">Teaching Resources</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/teachers/accessing-math-content-with-jaws-and-fusion/">Accessing Math Content with JAWS and Fusion</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/teachers/using-the-amazon-kindle-app-with-jaws/">Using the Amazon Kindle App with JAWS</a></li> <li><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/teachers/desmos-online-graphing-calculator/">Desmos Online Graphing Calculator</a></li> </ul> <h4 id="accessing-math-content-with-jaws-and-fusion-2">Accessing Math Content with JAWS and Fusion</h4> <p>JAWS® and Fusion® enable students to read and study math problems contained in web pages and Microsoft Word documents using both speech and braille. JAWS provides spoken, natural-language descriptions of math expressions using the same terms a teacher would use to explain them in a classroom. This enables students using JAWS or Fusion to read mathematical expressions as their sighted peers do.</p> <p>To interact with math, JAWS uses MathCAT to translate math content from web pages and Word documents to speech and Braille as well as offer numerous customization options. Currently, JAWS MathCAT support is only available for English.</p> <h5 id="math-on-web-pages-1">Math On Web Pages</h5> <p>JAWS supports reading math content in Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, and Mozilla Firefox that is created using MathML. MathML is a language for including mathematical content on web pages, enabling browsers to present math and science equations and formulas as they would appear on paper. Visit the <a href="https://www.w3.org/Math/">W3 website</a> to learn more about MathML and the tools used to add it to web pages.</p> <p>When you encounter MathML on a web page, JAWS describes the expression, followed by the message “math content.” If you are using a braille display and JAWS is configured for Contracted Braille, the message “Math” is displayed followed by the expression. If the expression is too long to fit on the display, you can use the panning buttons on your display to view the rest of it. Otherwise, if JAWS is set for Computer Braille, the message “Math” is displayed followed by a message stating that Contracted Braille must be enabled to view math content. Pressing ENTER while focused on the math content opens the Math Viewer where you can explore the expression in greater detail in both speech and braille. Check out the <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/content/html/jawshq/MathML-Samples.html">MathML Examples page</a> on the Freedom Scientific website to see how JAWS reads math content.</p> <p>Note: While not directly related to MathML, those involved with Statistical analysis may want to consider checking out <a href="https://blog.freedomscientific.com/fscast-183-using-the-sas-graphics-accelerator-to-listen-to-graphs-and-charts/">FSCast 183</a> which demonstrates some accessible tools for doing statistics.</p> <h5 id="math-in-microsoft-word-documents-1">Math in Microsoft Word Documents</h5> <p>In Microsoft Word, JAWS and Fusion supports reading math equations inserted into documents using one of the following methods:</p> <ul> <li>Math inserted using the options in the Symbols group of the Insert tab in the ribbon. JAWS does not require any third-party software or plugins be installed in order to read math inserted this way. Check out this article on the <a href="https://www.teachucomp.com/insert-equations-in-word-instructions/">TeachUcomp website</a> for instructions on inserting math into Word documents using this method. The <a href="https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/insert-mathematical-symbols-91a4b04c-84a8-4de9-bd13-8609e14bed58">Microsoft Support website</a> also contains information on inserting mathematical symbols.</li> <li>Math inserted using the JAWS Braille Math Editor. A braille display that includes a keyboard, such as the Focus, is required in order to use this feature.</li> <li>Math inserted using MathType, available as a purchase from <a href="http://www.wiris.com/en">Wiris.com</a>. To read math content in a Word document that was created using MathType, the MathType software must at least be installed as a trial on the computer running JAWS. Visit the <a href="http://www.dessci.com/en/products/mathtype/">Design Science website</a> for more details about MathType. When you encounter a math equation or formula in a Word document, JAWS reads the problem and then says, “Math Content.” You can then press the layered keystroke INSERT+SPACEBAR followed by EQUALS to open the JAWS Math Viewer so you can study the equation in greater detail. See our <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/Content/Documents/Other/NativeWordSampleMath.docx">Native Word Sample Math document</a> for examples of how JAWS and Fusion can enable students to access math content in Word. The math problems in this document were created using the built-in features in Word, so you do not need to install any additional software, such as MathType, to read these examples with JAWS.</li> </ul> <h5 id="studying-equations-in-the-math-viewer-1">Studying Equations in the Math Viewer</h5> <p>The JAWS Math Viewer lets you explore all of the parts of an equation in order to study it in detail. When focused on math content on a web page, press ENTER to open the current math problem in the Math Viewer. When focused on math in a Word document, use the layered keystroke INSERT+SPACEBAR followed by EQUALS.</p> <p>Once the Math Viewer is open, explore its contents using the following keystrokes:</p> <p>Description</p> <p>Command</p> <p>Move to next element</p> <p>RIGHT ARROW</p> <p>Move to previous element</p> <p>LEFT ARROW</p> <p>Zoom in on the current element to explore individual segments</p> <p>DOWN ARROW</p> <p>Zoom out of the current element</p> <p>UP ARROW</p> <p>Move between cells if focused in a table</p> <p>CTRL+ARROW keys or ALT+CTRL+ARROW keys</p> <p>Move back an element</p> <p>BACKSPACE</p> <p>Announce current location in element</p> <p>SPACEBAR</p> <p>Set Place Marker at current location in Math Viewer (not the same as JAWS PlaceMarkers feature on web pages)</p> <p>CTRL+1 through 0 on the number row</p> <p>Move to Place Marker 1 through 10</p> <p>1 through 0 on the number row</p> <p>Read Place Marker 1 through 10</p> <p>SHIFT+1 through 0 on the number row</p> <p>Exit the Math Viewer</p> <p>ESC or ALT+F4</p> <p>Additionally, the contents of the Math Viewer are displayed visually on the screen. As the equation is navigated, the current expression or partial expression is highlighted so a sighted teacher can easily tell what part of the expression is being spoken.</p> <p>When using a Braille display, the entire expression remains on the display as you use the ARROW keys to navigate parts of the expression. However, the cursor (dots 7 and 8) moves to the start of the partial expression that gains focus. Pressing a cursor router over a term in the expression will immediately move the focus to the specific location in the expression.</p> <p>Open the <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/content/html/jawshq/MathML-Samples.html">MathML Examples web page</a> or the <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/Content/Documents/Other/NativeWordSampleMath.docx">Native Word Sample Math document</a> and try exploring the various math expressions in the Math Viewer. Remember: Pressing ENTER opens the Math Viewer when focused on math content on web pages, and pressing INSERT+SPACEBAR followed by EQUALS opens the Math Viewer when focused on math content in Word documents.</p> <h5 id="selecting-a-braille-math-code-1">Selecting a Braille Math Code</h5> <p>If a refreshable braille display is connected, JAWS shows math expressions on the display using either Nemeth or Unified English Braille (UEB Math). To switch between Nemeth or UEB Math for displaying math content in the Math Viewer or Braille Math Editor, press INSERT+EQUALS. Focus display users can also press RIGHT SHIFT+DOTS 1-2-3-4-5-6 on the display’s keyboard to switch the math braille code.</p> <p>Since Nemeth and UEB Math are only available in English, make sure JAWS is configured for one of the English contracted braille output modes by doing the following:</p> <ul> <li>Press INSERT+6 on the number row to open Settings Center.</li> <li>To apply changes to all applications, press CTRL+SHIFT+D to load the JAWS default settings. To apply changes to a specific application, select it from the Applications combo box.</li> <li>In the Search edit box, type “Translation” without the quotes.</li> <li>Press DOWN ARROW to move to Translation in the filtered search results in the tree view and press ENTER to move focus to the Translation group. Press RIGHT ARROW to expand the group.</li> <li>In the Language combo box, make sure English – United States is selected.</li> <li>In the Output combo box, make sure one of the Grade 1 or Grade 2 options is selected.</li> <li>Select OK to save your changes and close Settings Center. Tip: If your student is using a Freedom Scientific <a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/braille/focus/">Focus Blue</a> braille display, you can press DOTS 1-2-4-5-7-8 CHORD to quickly switch to contracted braille.</li> </ul> <h5 id="entering-math-equations-using-the-jaws-braille-math-editor-1">Entering Math Equations using the JAWS Braille Math Editor</h5> <p>If you have access to a Braille display that also supports typing in braille and you are familiar with the Nemeth or UEB Math code for entering and reading math content, the Braille Math Editor in JAWS and Fusion enables you to input your own equations, and in Office 365, edit existing equations in Word documents. If you are new to <a href="https://nemeth.aphtech.org/">Nemeth</a> or <a href="https://uebmath.aphtech.org/">UEB Math</a>, check out these tutorials which teach these popular Braille codes beginning with the very basics up through advanced mathematics.</p> <p>To open the Math Editor, press the layered command INSERT+SPACEBAR followed by SHIFT+EQUALS (plus sign). Focus braille display users can also press DOTS 3-4-6-7 CHORD. Similar to reading math content, JAWS braille output must be set for one of the English Grade 1 or Grade 2 translation settings in order to launch the editor.</p> <p>When the Math Editor opens, focus is placed into an edit field where you can immediately begin typing the equation in Nemeth or UEB Math from your braille display’s keyboard. To switch between Braille math codes, press INSERT+EQUALS, or RIGHT SHIFT+DOTS 1-2-3-4-5-6 from a Focus Braille display. As you type, a preview pane below the edit field visually displays the equation so a sighted teacher or parent can review it. Once you are finished inputting the math equation, press ENTER or choose the Accept button to close the Math Editor. If you are in Word, the equation you entered is automatically inserted into the document at your current location. The equation is also copied to the Clipboard so you can paste it in other applications.</p> <p>Opening the Math Editor while focused on a math equation in a Word document displays the existing equation in the editor using the currently active Braille math code, allowing you to edit or replace it. After making any changes and pressing ENTER to close the editor, the current equation in the document is replaced by the new or modified equation.</p> <p>Note: After inserting or modifying an equation in Word from the Math Editor, the blinking cursor (dots 7 and 8) on the braille display always remains at the beginning of the math content, even as you move by character with the LEFT and RIGHT ARROW keys. If you need to insert another line of math content, first press the END key to move to the end of the current math content and then press ENTER.</p> <p>While the Math Editor is opened, you have the following additional options:</p> <ul> <li>Press CTRL+N to start a new equation.</li> <li>Press CTRL+P to preview the current equation in the Math Viewer. When finished, press ESC to return to the Math Editor.</li> <li>Press ALT+E to open the edit menu where you can copy your Braille input to the Clipboard using a specific format. MathML is the default format when copying, however, depending on the application where you intend to paste the equation, you can also choose to copy your content to LaTeX or Braille ASCII. After choosing a format to copy to, paste the equation into the specific application before pressing ENTER or selecting Accept to close the Math Editor as this always copies as MathML and will erase the current clipboard contents.</li> </ul> <h5 id="desmos-online-graphing-calculator-3">Desmos Online Graphing Calculator</h5> <p>The Desmos Graphing Calculator is a free online math tool widely used by teachers and students to plot equations and learn math concepts. Use it to plot data, graph functions, evaluate equations, and create classroom activities.</p> <p>Visit our <a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/teachers/desmos-online-graphing-calculator/">Desmos Online Graphing Calculator page</a> for an overview and tutorials.</p> <h3 id="ai-privacy-statement">AI Privacy Statement</h3> <h4 id="ai-privacy-statement-1">AI Privacy Statement</h4> <p>Freedom Scientific acts as a pass-through to Open AI’s Chat GPT and Anthropic Claude Enterprise Services. We, as well as our partners, do not store or train on any images that are sent through Picture Smart or screenshots of controls sent through the UI Labeler. We pass this content to either Chat GPT or Claude using the associated prompt only. In order to enhance the quality of our documentation, we retain queries and feedback provided by users through FSCompanion. For information about how Chat GPT and Claude process your information, please see the <a href="https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/">Open AI Enterprise Privacy page</a> and the <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms">Commercial Terms of Service  Anthropic</a>.</p> <p>View our full <a href="https://support.freedomscientific.com/privacy-policy/enu/">Complete Data Privacy Policy</a>.</p> <h5 id="contact-us-5">Contact Us</h5> <p>If you have questions about the privacy aspects of our Services or would like to make a complaint, please call 1-800-444-4443, ext. 1191 or email us at [email protected].</p> <h5 id="privacy-and-security-faq">Privacy and Security FAQ</h5> <h6 id="page-explorer-and-fscompanion">Page Explorer and FSCompanion</h6> <p>Q: What is the source of the AI model utilized with FSCompanion and Page Explorer?</p> <p>A: We use OpenAI’s enterprise LLM as the foundation, and we customize its behavior using Vispero’s proprietary data and system-level prompts.</p> <p>Q: Do you collect any of the website content submitted to Page Explorer for analysis?</p> <p>A: No. We do not collect or store any of the website content that the user submits for analysis.</p> <p>Q: Do you save the generated answer from Page Explorer?</p> <p>A: To improve Page Explorer, we temporarily store the generated response as part of the FSCompanion conversation data, along with any follow-up questions asked through the interface.</p> <p>Q: What data is collected?</p> <p>A: FSCompanion temporarily stores the text of user queries and user-submitted feedback to help improve the product experience. If available, we also collect general location information (such as country or region) to better understand where our tools are being used. This data is approximate and not linked to individual users.</p> <p>Q: Do you store any audio recordings?</p> <p>A: Audio from the FSCompanion dictation feature is not saved, only the transcribed text is stored for telemetry.</p> <p>Q: How long is user collected data stored in your database?</p> <p>A: Collected telemetry data is stored for a maximum of two years.</p> <p>Q: Can you confirm that customer-submitted queries are not used for model training purposes?</p> <p>A: Yes. The enterprise API from OpenAI utilized by Freedom Scientific is designed to prevent the storage or use of customer-submitted queries for model training. Customer questions are only sent to OpenAI for processing, such as transcribing audio dictation.</p> <p>Q: Can you verify the security of the communication channel between FSCompanion and the OpenAI model?</p> <p>A: Yes, all communication between FSCompanion and OpenAI is conducted over TLS, ensuring end-to-end secure communication.</p> <h6 id="picture-smart-ai-and-ai-based-ui-labeler">Picture Smart AI and AI Based UI Labeler</h6> <p>Q: What is the source of the AI models utilized with Picture Smart AI and the AI Based UI Labeler?</p> <p>A: Freedom Scientific leverages publicly accessible models from Anthropic and OpenAI, specifically through their enterprise-level APIs. While requests from Picture Smart AI are sent to both models, requests from the AI Based UI Labeler are sent only to OpenAI.</p> <p>Q: Can you confirm that customer-submitted image data is not used for model training purposes?</p> <p>A: Yes. The enterprise APIs from Anthropic and OpenAI utilized by Freedom Scientific are designed to prevent the storage or use of customer-submitted images for model training.</p> <p>Q: Specifically describe how an image is processed within your system.</p> <p>A: An image is processed by transmitting a combination of pre-defined system prompts, user-generated prompts, and configurable parameters like temperature to the respective API.</p> <p>Q: How is image data transferred from the JAWS application to your service, and from what infrastructure are the API calls executed, including what security measures are in place?</p> <p>A: Image data is transmitted directly from the JAWS application to the Freedom Scientific service. API calls originate from a secure Freedom Scientific backend, authenticated via access key management.</p> <p>Q: Detail the security protocols employed for communication between the JAWS application and your web service.</p> <p>A: All communication with the Freedom Scientific web service is secured using TLS connections over HTTPS (port 443).</p> <p>Q: What data retention policies are in place for image data within your service?</p> <p>A: The Freedom Scientific service maintains a temporary cache of image data and associated responses to support image-based chat functionality.</p> <p>Q: What is the duration of this temporary cache, and how is data purged?</p> <p>A: The cache is automatically cleared every four hours. No images are permanently stored.</p> <p>Q: Can you verify the security of the communication channel between your service and the Anthropic/OpenAI models?</p> <p>A: Yes, all communication between the Freedom Scientific service and Anthropic/OpenAI models is conducted over TLS, ensuring end-to-end secure communication.</p> <p>Q: Is it possible to disable the Picture Smart AI functionality during the setup?</p> <p>A: Yes, Picture Smart AI can be disabled during installation. See: <a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/training/enterprise/installation/#:~:text=IsPictureSmartEnabled%20%E2%80%93%20Set%20to%200%20to%20disable%20or,1%20to%20restrict%20Picture%20Smart%20to%20legacy%20functionality.">Software Installation Guide</a></p> <h3 id="arpa-relief-funding">ARPA Relief Funding</h3> <h4 id="arpa-relief-funding-1">ARPA Relief Funding</h4> <h5 id="arpa-relief-funding-prevent-learning-loss-close-achievement-gaps-and-increase-accessibility">ARPA Relief Funding: Prevent learning loss, close achievement gaps and increase accessibility</h5> <p>ARPA provides funds to libraries and schools to address student learning loss, close achievement gaps and assist with distance learning. Help support your students and patrons and increase accessibility by providing Assistive Technology with the help of ARPA and Freedom Scientific.</p> <h5 id="what-that-means">What That Means:</h5> <p>Schools and libraries will have access to funds to purchase assistive technology. The funds will be allocated by state and those states will have access to the funds throughout 2024. Now is the opportunity to review your current environment and plan for addressing in-person learning, distance learning or a hybrid approach.</p> <h5 id="how-can-we-help">How Can We Help?</h5> <p>Freedom Scientific has been providing students, schools, and libraries assistive technology, both hardware and software based, for over 30 years. Our innovative technology is designed to promote independence, allowing blind and low vision individuals the same access to information as their sighted peers. Our team is passionate about what we do and committed to the communities that we serve.</p> <h5 id="software-solutions">Software Solutions:</h5> <p>Freedom Scientific provides superior software solutions for blind and low vision needs. Our world-renowned JAWS screen reading software, ZoomText screen magnification software and Fusion provide users the independence and ability to seek education and obtain or maintain a career after vision loss. JAWS and ZoomText are considered the industry standard and can be widely found in the schools, universities, and the workplace.</p> <h6 id="meet-mitchell-a-freedom-scientifics-student-of-the-month">Meet Mitchell, a Freedom Scientific’s Student of the Month</h6> <h5 id="hardware-solutions">Hardware Solutions:</h5> <p>Our expansive product line includes both low vision and blindness technology for all aspects of daily living. Our wide range of portable and desktop magnifiers such as the RUBY, TOPAZ, and ONYX are designed for their ease of use and assist with daily activities at home or school. Our impressive line of blindness hardware products include refreshable Braille displays which can connect to computers, tablets, and mobile phones. Scanning and reading devices convert printed material into audio files and braille. These solutions offer many options tailored to fit an individual’s needs.</p> <h5 id="suggested-solutions-for-your-school-or-library">Suggested Solutions for your School or Library</h5> <ul> <li>TOPAZ Ultra: Easy to carry from room to room. 3-in-1 camera for near, distance and self-view</li> <li>Fusion: Best of JAWS screen reading and ZoomText magnification in one software package</li> <li>Omni Reader: Reads printed text to you, magnifies small objects and can connect to braille display</li> <li>RUBY: Handheld magnifier that is perfect for spot reading with contrast and 2x-13x magnification</li> <li>Focus 40: Refreshable braille display with Bluetooth connectivity for up to 5 devices (tablet, smart phone, computer)</li> </ul> <h5 id="training-resources-1">Training Resources</h5> <p>We have a dedicated training resources section on our website where you can easily find things such as online video tutorials, live and recorded webinars, JAWS teaching modules, documentation, and weekly podcasts. All can be found at: www.freedomscientific.com/training.</p> <p>You can also visit the Freedom Scientific Training YouTube channel to view more training videos on our software. Check it out at <a href="https://www.youtube.com/FreedomScientificTraining">youtube.com</a></p> <h5 id="reach-out-to-us-to-learn-more-about-how-freedom-scientific-can-assist-you-with-learning-loss-helping-to-close-achievement-gaps-and-assist-with-distance-learning.">Reach out to us to learn more about how Freedom Scientific can assist you with learning loss, helping to close achievement gaps and assist with distance learning.</h5> <p>ARPA Relief Funding: The American Rescue Plan Act</p> <p>ARPA provides funds to libraries and schools to address student learning loss, close achievement gaps and assist with distance learning. Help support your students and patrons and increase accessibility by providing Assistive Technology with the help of ARPA and Freedom Scientific.</p> <p>What That Means:</p> <p>Schools and libraries will have access to funds to purchase assistive technology. The funds will be allocated by state and those states will have access to the funds through the end of 2024. Now is the opportunity to review your current environment and plan for addressing in-person learning, distance learning or a hybrid approach.</p> <p>How Can We Help?</p> <p>Freedom Scientific has been providing students, schools, and libraries assistive technology, both hardware and software based, for over 30 years. All can be found at www.freedomscientific.com/training</p> <ul> <li>TOPAZ Video Magnifier: Excellent for productivity. Magnification up to 67x (depending on monitor size)</li> <li>Fusion: Best of JAWS screen reading and ZoomText magnification in one software package</li> <li>RUBY: Handheld magnifier that is perfect for spot reading with contrast and 2x-13x magnification</li> <li>Focus 40: Refreshable braille display with Bluetooth connectivity for up to 5 devices (tablet, smart phone, computer) Reach out to us to learn more about how Freedom Scientific can assist you with learning loss, close achievement gaps and assist with distance learning.</li> </ul> <h3 id="careers-miscellaneous">Careers (Miscellaneous)</h3> <h4 id="careers-1">Careers</h4> <p><a href="https://vispero.rec.pro.ukg.net/FRE1500FRDS/JobBoard/bdb17a81-bb2f-47ee-8877-adbc6b5ecbc6/?q=&o=postedDateDesc">View Job Listings</a></p> <h5 id="are-you-looking-for-a-rewarding-career-where-your-contributions-truly-make-a-difference">Are you looking for a rewarding career where your contributions truly make a difference?</h5> <p>Working at Vispero you will be part of a global team known for being the world’s leading assistive technology provider for the blind and visually impaired. id="ccpa-request-webform">CCPA Request Webform</h3> <h4 id="ccpa-request-webform-1">CCPA Request Webform</h4> <p>California Residents may use this form to exercise their CCPA rights: opt-out of sale; access your information; and delete your information.</p> <p>If you are a resident of California, and you want to submit a request to Vispero under the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), please fill out the webform below. Required fields are marked with an asterisk.* We will contact you at the email or phone number listed below if we have questions regarding your request.</p> <p>Our Privacy Practices: For general information about how we handle personal information of California residents, please visit our <a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/privacy-policy">Privacy Policy</a> and the section on Important Information for California Residents.</p> <p>Sale: California residents have the right to opt-out of the “Sale” of their personal information. California defines the term “Sale” broadly, and includes, our selling, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring or otherwise communicating (collectively a “Sale”) of your personal information to another business or third party for monetary or other valuable consideration. For general information about our sale of personal information and more details about your right to opt-out of any sale, please visit our <a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/privacy-policy">privacy policy</a>.</p> <p>Agents: If you are an agent submitting a request, please complete this form, print out a copy, and email the form along with your power of attorney or notarized authorization from the consumer to us at [email protected]. We may contact the consumer to verify your authority and/or to authenticate the consumer.</p> <p>Additional Questions: If you have questions about this webform, please contact us at [email protected]. If you do not wish to use this webform, you can submit your request by calling us at 1-800-444-4443, ext 1191.</p> <h3 id="connect-with-vispero-at-the-41st-annual-csun-assistive-technology">Connect With Vispero at the 41st Annual CSUN Assistive Technology</h3> <h4 id="connect-with-vispero-at-the-41st-annual-csun-assistive-technology-1">Connect With Vispero at the 41st Annual CSUN Assistive Technology</h4> <p>The Vispero hardware team is looking forward to joining the assistive technology community at the <a href="https://conference.csun.at/event/2026/summary">41st Annual CSUN Assistive Technology Conference</a>, taking place March 9–13, 2026 at the Marriott Anaheim in Anaheim, CA.</p> <p>CSUN is an important opportunity to connect, exchange ideas, and explore how accessible technology continues to evolve. We invite you to meet with the team at our booth, attend educational sessions, and experience our latest product innovations firsthand.</p> <h5 id="visit-us-in-the-exhibit-hall">Visit Us in the Exhibit Hall</h5> <p>Booth 503 – Marquis Ballroom Exhibit Hall</p> <ul> <li>Meet Our Sales & Product Team: <ul> <li>Richard Tapping, James Bailey, Joe McDaniel, Jeff Bazer and Patrick Murphy</li> </ul></li> <li>Product Demonstrations: <ul> <li>Hands-on demonstrations of Enhanced Vision, Optelec, and Freedom Scientific products including: <ul> <li>Focus 640</li> <li>Merlin Pro</li> <li>DaVinci Pro</li> <li>Onyx OCR</li> <li>Clearview C Speech</li> <li>Merlin Mini 17″</li> <li>Ruby 10″ Speech</li> <li>Ruby XL 5″ HD</li> <li>Ruby 7″ HD</li> <li>Compact 10″ Speech</li> <li>Compact 8″</li> <li>Smart Reader HD</li> <li>Amigo 8″</li> </ul></li> </ul></li> <li>YETI Hopper Soft Cooler Giveaway</li> <li>Swag and more!</li> </ul> <h5 id="vispero-thought-leadership">Vispero Thought Leadership</h5> <p>Platinum 2 – Marriott Ballroom</p> <p>Vispero will host live educational sessions throughout the conference focused on product innovation, accessibility best practices, and real-world applications of assistive technology. These sessions are designed to provide practical takeaways, product updates, and insight into how Vispero is shaping the future of accessible hardware.</p> <h6 id="tuesday-march-10-2026">Tuesday, March 10, 2026</h6> <ul> <li>1:20 PM – 2:00 PM: Digital Accessibility: Legal Update & Hot Topics (David Sloan)</li> <li>2:20 PM – 3:00 PM: Vispero & Everway: Scaling Enterprise Solutions for Inclusive Workplaces (Matt Ater)</li> </ul> <h6 id="wednesday-march-11-2026">Wednesday, March 11, 2026</h6> <ul> <li>9:20 AM – 10:00 AM: Using JAWS Inspect as a Screen Reader User Experience Design Tool (Jan Williams)</li> <li>10:20 AM – 11:00 AM: What’s New and Coming Up in JAWS, ZoomText, and Fusion (Ryan Jones & Nathan Romney)</li> <li>11:20 AM – 12:00 PM: AI & Web Accessibility in 2026: A Progress Report (Shaun Ryan & Omar Wahby)</li> <li>1:20 PM – 2:00 PM: Designing the Accessible Campus: Strategies for Inclusive Learning Experiences in 2026 (Cord Keating)</li> <li>2:20 PM – 3:00 PM: The Please be sure to include as much information as possible.</p> <p>Quality Department</p> <h3 id="covid-19-update">COVID-19 Update</h3> <h4 id="covid-19-update-1">COVID-19 Update</h4> <h5 id="us-update-june-4-2020">US Update: June 4, 2020</h5> <p>As the country slowly starts to ease restrictions, we know it is important to provide customers and partners with a transparent update on how we are responding. Ensuring the safety of our employees and their families is our top priority, which in turn protects our customers. We are committed to providing our customers with a service level they are accustomed to and have a clear understanding of what to expect going forward.</p> <h6 id="up-to-now">Up to now:</h6> <p>We have continued throughout this crisis to be fully operational with no incidents of COVID-19. Our fast planning back in early March to COVID-19 enabled us to adapt to the changing environment. Fortunately, our Clearwater offices in Florida were well prepared to work remotely given our Hurricane Preparedness plans and we were able to quickly transition to “work-from-home” format.</p> <p>In our manufacturing and logistics center in Huntington Beach, CA we added multiple shifts for social distancing and provided protective equipment for our employees. These measures, together with an employee commitment to practice social distancing and taking the CDC recommended precautions, ensured the safety of our employees, partners and customers.</p> <h6 id="what-is-next">What is next?</h6> <p>As customers and institutions implement strategies to open, Vispero is stepping up our commitment to ongoing safety measures. Vispero will conduct demos and visits by appointment only. We are providing increased protection for our employees and partners with Personal Protection (PPE) Kits that include gloves, masks, face shields, gowns, and hand sanitizer.</p> <p>As part of this safety measure, Vispero is also providing cleaning and disinfecting equipment guidelines and materials to partners to ensure maximum protection as the restrictions begin to relax.</p> <p>We will continue to monitor the situation and adapt as necessary to ensure we are doing what is best for our employees and partners. As always, we appreciate your business and your continued support.</p> <p><a href="https://www.freedomscientific.com/Content/Pdfs/Cleaning-and-Disinfecting-Vispero-Low-Vision-and-Blindness-Products.pdf">Cleaning and Disinfecting Vispero Low Vision and Blindness Products</a></p> <h5 id="us-update-march-17-2020">US Update: March 17, 2020</h5> <p>As COVID-19 (the coronavirus) continues to impact the global community, we know it is important to provide customers and partners with a transparent update on how we are responding to the outbreak. Ensuring the safety of our employees and their families is our top priority which in turn protects our customers. We are committed to providing our customers with a service level they are accustomed to receiving from us and that they have a clear understanding of what to expect as outlined below.</p> <ul> <li>Business Continuity: We are continuing our business operations in a responsible way. Vispero has operated with a strong workforce for years and is fully set up to continue operations remotely in accordance with recommended health guidelines with minimal disruption. Our customers will continue to receive similar levels of communication and service they have come to expect.</li> <li>Business Travel: We are pausing all business travel to customer locations for onsite activities until further notice. We will be converting those meetings to virtual meetings using conference and video calls. We are monitoring the situation and will return to normal travel operations when guidance allows. Where feasible, we will offer options to convert onsite services to digital or remote delivery and will be communicating individually if this applies to your account.</li> <li>Events & Conferences: We have canceled our onsite participation at conferences, tradeshows, and events until conditions support a return to those operations. We don’t know how long this outbreak will last and will return to our normal presence when it is safe to do so. In the interim, we will provide digital delivery of any webinars or other content so that you may continue to get value from our participation.</li> <li>Communications: We will provide transparency through this process. Because we are continuing business operations in our remote capacity, you may continue to reach out to your usual business contact and expect similar response times. With many school closings, some of our employees do have families in self-quarantine at home and may result in hearing children and families in the background. Please be assured that we are continually reviewing the situation and adapting as necessary to ensure we are doing what is best for our employees and the business. We will continue to provide updates as the situation is constantly changing. Thank you for your business and continued support.</li> </ul> <h3 id="csun24">CSUN24</h3> <h4 id="csun24-1">CSUN24</h4> <h4 id="get-your-free-90-day-software-license">Get Your Free 90-Day Software License</h4> <p>Thank you for your interest in the Fusion Suite and for visiting us at the CSUN 2024 conference.
